entries.title: Seeing Through the Lightness
entries.summary: Equanimity once defined Brice Marden’s art—optical balance so solid it felt inevitable. In a current survey, maintaining it feels more like a feat, something grabbed in motion.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
Hanging nearby at Gagosian, Point (1969) spreads the same enigmatic, inviting surface across three panels in different flavors of green. Beyond perceptual experiments, Marden exploits the strange power of color to carry us, as scent does, to other places and times. Tiffany Bell’s newly published catalogue raisonné of Marden’s paintings tells us that Point is to Point Lobos, California, as Nebraska is to Nebraska, but the painted panels don’t dictate a location, just a certain quality of light. Summer Table (1972–1973) takes its hues from the Greek island of Hydra, but stripped of local landmarks, its triad of pale blue, deep yellow, and cool slate can summon sea and sun across many longitudes.

The thirty-one paintings on view in “Brice Marden: I Am Plane Image” constitute the most substantive New York survey of Marden’s career since MoMA’s retrospective twenty years ago. Drawn from museums, private collections, and the artist’s estate, they run from numinous monochromes that established his reputation in the 1960s to a scrappy ten-foot-long color sequence, his last work. The installation is spacious and stately—Gagosian in its most eloquent kunsthalle mode—while the paintings themselves are by turns mesmerizing, elegiac, and exhilarating. But the most pressing reason to make the trip to Chelsea is to be reminded, face-to-face with Marden’s paintings, that “knowing” them through JPEGs isn’t knowing them at all.

Works that in reproduction look like tiny hard-edge abstractions reveal themselves as chunky constructions with stained canvas edges and visibly irregular paint application. The handmadeness is always apparent, even as his constructions became more complex, with multiple color blocks and columns arranged in parallel, or in post-and-lintel structures that can suggest the solemnity of ancient colonnades or the confidence of Sixth Avenue modernism. The heroic, euphonious, twelve-panel Number One (1983–1984) shows an artist in complete control of his medium. But it’s hard to shake the feeling that as the canvases got bigger, the questions posed about the experience of looking got smaller. It can be a short hop from complete control of your medium to boredom with your own mastery.

“I Am Plane Image” limits itself to painting, but the change that overtook Marden’s art in the mid-1980s was rooted in works on paper. Much has been written about how smitten he was by the mix of precision and accident he saw in Japanese calligraphy, how he studied Chinese calligraphy (whose romance with unraveling runs deeper) and took to drawing with long sticks that reduced control by amplifying inadvertent motion. Line, however, had always been part of his visual thinking. Years before he picked up those sticks, he had worked on window designs for Basel’s medieval minster, considering color along with line segments and how to define a structure to be both looked at and looked through. Earlier still, his drawings and etchings employed a dynamic, exploratory line not seen in his paintings. (Some of that evidence can be seen at Print Center New York, where Marden’s 1972 portfolio Ten Days appears in “Parasol Press: Breaking New Ground,” on view through December 19, 2026.)

One can know all of this and still be startled by the leap from the settled poise of Number One to the tumult of 4 (Bone) (1987–1988), where all the action collapses into a single canvas, the surface judders with pentimenti, and the defining structure is a twitchy line folding in on itself like a jungle gym mangled by a steamroller. In the first of his grand Cold Mountain paintings, begun in 1988 and named for the reclusive Tang dynasty poet Han Shan, Marden’s gray line, liquid yet angular, tumbles in nine-foot columns like inclement weather.

Equanimity had been the defining trait of Marden’s art—optical balance so solid it felt inevitable. In the new paintings, by contrast, maintaining balance feels more like an athletic feat, something grabbed in motion. Eventually the jagged angles of 4 (Bone) softened into balletic curves, and his palette blossomed afresh. In Study for the Muses (Eagles Mere Version) (1991–1994/1997–1999), skeins of pink, green, and blue, smooth as rubber bands, wiggle across a pale backdrop filled with the shadows of earlier skeins and discarded plans. But the illusion of catching something on the fly remained.

Though Marden is often categorized as a minimalist (two decades of monochrome panels will have that effect), he always said he felt closer to the Abstract Expressionists. But that label doesn’t feel quite right either: Expressionism usually denotes a visual language for sharing emotions. Marden’s method was to distill one visual experience into another. The thrill of a mysterious green in Nebraska becomes the rapture of green in Nebraska. His art also carries little of the Angst-und-Traum baggage of Ab Ex. He could paint darkly when he wanted, but mostly he didn’t. Nothing is stable. Everything is OK.

Advertisement

At the time of the MoMA retrospective, Marden’s career still read as a drama in two acts: first the finely tuned color blocks, then the autographic gestures and glyphs. Critics pointed out threads of continuity—the tender chromatic nuance, the deliberate distance between hand and mark (whether through assiduously smoothed layers or a long stick)—but the break was real. Once there had been autonomous planes of color, now there was figure and ground: things (albeit abstract things) on top of other things.

At Gagosian, where almost half the paintings postdate the MoMA exhibition, that break feels less eventful, its before and after more tightly knit together. In The Propitious Garden of Plane Image, Second Version (2000–2006), system and squiggle march hand in hand: six color panels arranged in ROYGBIV sequence are each home to looping bands of color such that the background color of one panel turns up in the frontmost loop in the next panel, then cedes the foreground in the next—an order you sense before you recognize it as a pattern.

Panels of unbroken color make a comeback, as does that early drip strip at the bottom of Nebraska, now expanded to occupy the bottom quarter or so of vertical canvases. Marden cited Donald Judd’s spatial parsing and Mark Rothko’s top-heavy cadence as models, but the format also recalls the narrative predellas that foot Renaissance altarpieces, filling in the backstory of the image above (as, in a sense, Marden’s scruffy, splattered ones do). He used this new structure for monochromes (there’s a whole phylum dedicated to the translucent mineral pigment terre verte), and he also filled that upper space with line—sometimes as dense as window grates, sometimes loose and capricious. Like the paths of GPS-tracked wildlife, his line always looks purposeful, even if that purpose eludes us.

In Rivers (2020–2021) both sections are washed in effulgent green light. The lower part, a shade yellower, has the mottled look of a forest in fog. Above, a handful of blue ribbons traverse ground the color of lichen. Traces of a penciled grid hint at submerged cartography or craquelure. I’ve no idea which rivers Marden had in mind, if indeed the title refers to actual bodies of water. Standing in front of it, however, I was suddenly, vividly, taken back to a rain-soaked afternoon in a tea shop in the mountains above Taipei, looking out at jungle through steamed-up windows.

Marden’s allegiance to the truth of a flat surface—the “plane image”—never faltered. Yet allusions to places and things outside the canvas are everywhere. His titles name-check locations from Nebraska to Santorini and nod to art history, Greek mythology, and Christian theology. A vitrine of objects from his studio is an invitation to go motif hunting, seeking echoes of the zigzag pattern of a sea snail shell, or the ticktock of light and shadow in a snapshot of Marden at the Acropolis, or the elusive glaze of a Ru ware bowl stand from the Song dynasty, imperfectly reported on a postcard.

The title of the exhibition in which Rivers first appeared was “These paintings are of themselves” (2021), which reads as a preemptive rebuttal to any damp tea shop musings. The title of his previous exhibition, however, was “It reminds me of something, and I don’t know what it is” (2019). Great painters have always managed to make objects in which both truths—a physically circumscribed collection of pigments, and some ineffable other—carry equal weight. When one looks at Marden’s art now, it’s clear that, from Nebraska on down, his work was never a celebration of autonomy; it was an atlas of connection.

entries.title: ‘Quest Without End’
entries.summary: The Scottish journalist Cal Flyn travels the world in search of the feelings that wild and abandoned places evoke.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
In the eighth or ninth century, around three hundred years after the abandonment of the Roman temple and bath complex of Aquae Sulis (today’s Bath, England), an anonymous Anglo-Saxon wandering the lichen-covered rubble was inspired to compose an elegy now known as “The Ruin.” The poet had no idea of the origin of the ruins, or who could have built them, and perhaps this is why the poem contains the sense of wonder of a character in a science fiction novel encountering a trace of an ancient and extinct intergalactic civilization:

This masonry is wondrous; fates broke it…

the work of giants is decaying…

Bright were the castle buildings, many the bathing halls…

death took all the brave men away…

In time the elegy itself became a ruin, the single surviving copy disfigured with a burn mark that obliterates many of the words.

The contemplation of ruins is surely one of humanity’s most enduring and enjoyable, if melancholic, pastimes. Rose Macaulay’s 1953 classic, Pleasure of Ruins, is perhaps nonpareil, offering a global overview of the debris of vanished civilizations in her own words as well as those of writers from Petrarch to Henry James. Macaulay emphasizes that, oftentimes, the more mysterious ruins are, the greater their emotional impact. “No circumstance so forcibly marks the desolation of a spot once inhabited, as the prevalence of Nature over it,” she writes, quoting Thomas Whately. She continues:

We might be still more delighted to see Troy or Athens, Corinth, Paestum or Rome, as they stood two thousand odd years ago; but that cannot be; this broken beauty is all we have of that ancient magnificence; we cherish it like the extant fragments of some lost and noble poem.

The Scottish journalist Cal Flyn is one of many more recent writers who have examined the effects that ruins can have on us. In Islands of Abandonment (2022), she explores the hills near her home in Scotland, which she learns are composed of burned oil shale waste; postindustrial landscapes in the northeastern US; European battlefields; and Chernobyl, which she describes as “the most radioactive environment on Earth.” In these places she finds new life, beauty, and enchantment. “To come into an abandoned mine or spoil heap or quarry or parking lot or oil terminal, and to see it for the natural wonderland it has become is, I admit, a difficult ask,” she writes. “But in these environmentally straitened days, it is a taste worth cultivating.”

Flyn’s detailed and sometimes digressive histories of abandoned sites can be a strength, as when she explains the fate of an area near Verdun, France, where what appeared to be an idyllic clearing was found in 2007 to contain shockingly high levels of arsenic and other heavy metals from the chemical weapons that had been buried and forgotten there after World War I. But it can also be a weakness, for while the book conveys many astonishing and little-known stories, its more didactic passages can dilute the pure amazement generated by the contemplation of ruins. Our imaginations, when unconstrained by walls of fact, can create marvels like Shelley’s “Ozymandias,” as well as the more humble but gratifying reimaginings of the past that we all construct in our heads when visiting historical sites.

Flyn’s new book, The Savage Landscape, is almost the opposite of Islands of Abandonment in that it focuses on Earth’s least altered landscapes. But like Flyn’s earlier book it enters a crowded field. Jay Griffiths’s Wild: An Elemental Journey (2006)—which documents a seven-year journey to the world’s most remote places, from the polar caps to the tropical rainforests of Indonesian Papua, where Griffiths lived among tribal peoples—is just one example of excellent work that has trod similar ground.

In The Savage Landscape Flyn leads us to the deserts of Sinai and the depths of the oceanic abyss, and on to a globe-spanning journey to some of the world’s most famous and remote wild places. For Flyn, wilderness is very personal. She goes there to live “more intensely,” and in doing so, she says, she finds “a calmness and a clarity often missing from the rest of my life.” Flyn shares with William Henry Jackson, Ansel Adams, and other pioneers of the American wilderness movement a preoccupation with the feelings that the experience of being in the wild evokes. Yet The Savage Landscape’s overall structure mirrors that of Islands of Abandonment, including much factual material concerning wildlife management and other issues.

Flyn begins in the Colorado Rockies. There, on a lonely horse trail several days’ ride from the nearest town, she encounters a sign proclaiming “Welcome to the Holy Cross Wilderness,” below which is a register inviting hikers to “sign in.” Flyn’s sense of freedom and self-sufficiency evaporates in the face of this bureaucratic intrusion. Only later does she realize that she had stumbled upon “the central paradox at the heart of the wilderness preservation movement: the problem of translating a subjective response to landscape into real terms.”

Advertisement

It is to the wilderness of Mt. Sinai, Egypt, that Flyn leads us next. This is a land into which mystics and prophets have wandered for millennia, seeking a different way of being in the world. She joins a group of hikers ascending the holy mountain at night, and as she sits near the summit in the pre-dawn, she tries to understand the qualities of the various wildernesses sought by spiritual hermits. She decides that such places must be largely “natural,” populated by wild creatures and isolated from humanity, though they may also serve as hangouts for “wild men.” As she grapples with these definitions, she asks what is it exactly that she, Cal Flyn, is looking for? Before an answer comes, the flat light of day dispels whatever mystical atmosphere she had discerned in the panorama. Ejected from her self-defined wilderness, she joins the descending crowd as they pick their way across the rocky and rapidly heating landscape.

Seeking to understand the people who give themselves to the wilderness, she visits the Monastery of St. Paul the Anchorite, where she meets Salib, one of the monks, who agrees to show her around. His monastic life offers “a specific feeling,” he says, and when he becomes troubled in his mind, he walks into the wilderness until clarity finds him. Flyn admits that she “flirts with membership” in a group of wilderness purists who long for places “untouched by the original sin of the Anthropocene.” She also confesses to being astounded by Salib’s worldly air, and especially by his possession of a smartphone, which he checks several times as they walk the monastery grounds.

From Egypt we are transported to the wilds of Transylvania. Led by a tracker and researcher named Dan Marin, Flyn enters the Făgăraş Mountains, which encompass the region most remote from human settlements in all of Europe. Here thrives what is left of Europe’s mega-carnivores: brown bears, wolves, and lynx. Once, in the aftermath of the Black Death, all of Europe might have been like this, Flyn speculates. As the humans died and landscapes were abandoned, the carnivores settled the newly vacated lands, multiplying and becoming bold enough to enter what settlements there were, killing livestock and even vulnerable people such as unaccompanied children. Thus, in a seemingly unholy transformation, they began to challenge the biblically granted mantle of supremacy that, according to the people of the Book, had long been reserved for the sons of Adam.

As Europe’s human population recovered, the balance tipped back in humanity’s favor. We humans are vengeful, and have long memories. So the carnivores were persecuted and exterminated in region after region, until by the nineteenth century only Europe’s frozen north and highest mountains provided refuges for them. Were it not for the Romanian dictator Nicolae Ceaușescu, even the Făgăraş may have been emptied of its meat-eating megafauna. But during his tenure (1965–1989) he made bear hunting illegal for everyone except himself and a favored few. He even fed the bears, hoping to breed enormous specimens that could be shot and stuffed to adorn his residences.

For decades people have fed Romania’s bears, initially to provide specimens to be conveniently shot by the dictator and later as tourist attractions. During the one bear feeding I attended, our small group was shepherded into a blind just before dusk. There was a frisson of danger in the air as our armed guards pointed out the carcass of a goat pegged to the ground, surrounded by waste vegetables. Out of the gloaming at the forest’s edge, hunched, shaggy forms emerged one by one and began to feed. Much food remained after they were satiated, and the bears stuck about the blind. At 8:30 PM, a bored-looking guard glanced at his watch, stood up, and ushered us outside, leading us nonchalantly behind the bears to our car, which was waiting in the darkness a few hundred meters away. The frisson I enjoyed earlier had entirely evaporated.

Flyn’s experience of the Făgăraş bears was very different. As she walks a mountain trail with her guide, they pass paw prints and piles of bear dung, the freshness of which scares her. Later she meets Stefan, a ranger in the Făgăraş, who takes her to a lonely hut where he shows her images on his phone of the dead body of a shepherd who had lost a battle with a bear. She writes, “I felt myself shaken, but there was something else in there, too, a sort of horrified delight.” He flips to a video of the body of another shepherd that had been severely mutilated by a bear. Then he uncovers his right arm, which from armpit to forearm is marked with horrific scars: “Bear attack, he said.”

Advertisement

But for Flyn the most terrifying of all her encounters in the Făgăraş are those with the dogs kept by shepherds. Known as Ciobănesc Românesc Carpatin, they are about the size of St. Bernards, but rangier and shaggier. Each shepherd has a pack of around a dozen, and they are trained to go for the throat, without a thought for their own safety. They are a far greater danger to the wilderness hiker than bears and wolves. As she approaches a shepherd’s hut and is confronted by the dogs, Flyn reflects, “In our war with the wild…we have resorted to such vicious tactics and accepted bedfellows so violent that one is forced to wonder who the real villains are.” Fear, Flyn concludes, is part of what we’re looking for when we go into the woods.

Flyn’s fear of bears is widely shared by urban Europeans. It’s a fear that is often first learned, and then passed down, in fairy tales, and amplified by lurid accounts of the rare contemporary bear attack in the media.* Paradoxically, many people who share this fear applaud the conservation of lions in Africa and tigers in Asia, giving little thought to the people who must coexist with these mega-carnivores. Just whose landscape is savage and to whom is a paradox built into the title of Flyn’s book.

Flyn next turns to the Niassa Special Reserve in Mozambique to learn about contemporary wildlife conservation in Africa. Many conservation areas are funded through fees paid by trophy hunters. “You can kill almost anything if you are willing to pay,” Flyn explains, citing the case of Texas oil heir Corey Knowlton, who reputedly paid $350,000 “for the pleasure of killing a critically endangered black rhino.” The typical trophy hunter is a “white, American, dyed-in-the-wool Republican,” claims Flyn, who joins an American neurosurgeon in his seventies who wants to kill a Cape buffalo. “It is a true sportsman’s trial,” the man says, and Flyn concurs, noting that professional hunters and trackers die every year in pursuit of their trophies.

Soon after the neurosurgeon and Flyn leave camp, trackers pick up the spoor of an old bull marked for sacrifice. Flyn finds tracking the animal through the dense scrub a hair-raising experience: “Visibility had shrunk to a few metres at best,” she writes. “We might have been standing right next to the buffalo and never known it.” The trail is lost, and the hunt must be taken up the following day. Yet the hunter is satisfied, claiming that it’s all in the chase, and that he doesn’t much mind whether he shoots an animal anymore. (He did, finally, get his Cape buffalo.)

Back in camp after that first unsuccessful chase, Flyn meets a man she calls Trent. He’s a trophy hunter from Oklahoma, who shows her photographs of his trophy room, replete with numerous antelope heads and a whole, stuffed crocodile. Trent is altogether a more worrying type. He waits silently in blinds, his scent concealed by an ozone machine. “Like chemical warfare,” he says. Then we learn that Trent has bought his son an assault rifle for his birthday, along with a place in a training course run by former Navy SEALs who “talked very interestingly about shooting people.”

As distasteful as trophy hunting is to many, Flyn emphasizes that the money it provides is vital to the maintenance of many African conservation areas. Indeed, so closely is it entangled with conservation, she says, that “it’s not clear they can be separated and survive.” And the evidence is that the approach is working. Niassa’s lion population is one of the few on the continent that is growing, and countries that allow trophy hunting are doing better at conserving their wildlife than those that don’t.

There are other conservation models in Africa that involve the displacement of ethnic minorities for the sake of animals. Such is the fate of the Batwa people of Uganda: formerly known as “pygmies,” their homeland was the “Impenetrable Forest” of the Virunga Mountains, parts of which now form the Bwindi and Mgahinga National Parks. In the late 1980s and early 1990s these last remnants of rainforest were surrounded by farms owned by Tutsi and Hutu people, and according to Flyn they tended to view the diminutive Batwa as wild animals: “The Batwa wore skins and hunted with bows,” she explains. “They did not use money. Nor did they, generally, see the need for it. They lived in a different world with different values, albeit one only next door.”

It was the mountain gorilla that was the ultimate cause of the expulsion of the Batwa from their lands. By 1990 the Impenetrable Forest that was the common home of the Batwa and the mountain gorilla had shrunk by 70 percent. Something had to be done, the authorities decided, to save the gorillas. Chased from the forest by soldiers, the Batwa ran for their lives and ended up homeless, stateless, and landless. The government set aside a $4.3 million compensation fund, but the money disappeared—“probably embezzled,” Flyn says. Now the Batwa “cling to the edges of the forests they once called home,” Flyn writes, “scraping by as beggars or as indentured labourers for the very farmers who frayed their forest’s edges—and who live barely above subsistence level themselves.”

“Conservation refugees are, in some sense, human sacrifices to nature,” says Flyn. Yet in the case of the Batwa it was a sacrifice in vain: they didn’t even hunt the mountain gorilla. If they had been included in the conservation project, as has been done in places like Papua New Guinea, where the Tenkile Conservation Alliance works with over forty villages to protect tree kangaroos, they may have become excellent allies against the hunters and poachers who infest the gorillas’ habitat and continue to kill the apes.

The failure to include the Batwa was perhaps due in part to the attitude of the American zoologist Dian Fossey, who had been studying mountain gorillas since the 1960s with the encouragement of the anthropologist Louis Leakey. Her work was vital in transforming our view of gorillas from monsters to gentle giants. By the time she arrived in the Impenetrable Forest in the 1960s, wildlife hunting had been banned there for decades. Yet that ban was never enforced, and over the next twenty years the number of gorillas dropped from 480 to 260.

Fossey decided to enforce the ban herself, using vigilante methods that grew ever more extreme. She once caught a Batwa “poacher,” spread-eagled him, and lashed him with stinging nettles on the genitals and other sensitive parts. “I never knew that such little fellows had such big things,” she wrote to a friend. Eventually Fossey became “drunk, paranoid and alienated,” finally dying in her cabin in the forest from a machete wound that cleaved her skull. The murderer was never found.

In remote, lawless parts of Africa “conservationists have turned to aggressive military-style tactics” to protect wildlife from criminal organizations, writes Flyn. And certainly guns, drones, and other belligerent methods are needed if rhinos, for example, are to be protected from professional poachers.

There is a great moral issue here, but Flyn’s book is about wilderness, and she avoids the question of whether areas thus protected can be considered “wilderness” in any way. This is perhaps because The Savage Landscape takes only a shallow perspective on the past, rarely going beyond the last few centuries. Africa, however, is the cradle of humanity, and humans and their ancestors have been hunting big game there for at least two million years. More importantly, for at least as long, human clans have been defending our territories from rival clans’ “poachers.” So in that sense, both trophy hunting and militant conservation are parts of a very long tradition. It seems to me that because humans are a native species in Africa, we must consider all of the continent as wilderness, or none of it. Sadly, it’s a subject Flyn ignores.

Everywhere outside Africa, humans are a self-introduced species, and a different and even more troubling definition of wilderness has taken hold. It has its origins in the national parks movement in the US, which began with the creation of Yellowstone National Park in 1872. “The national park has been celebrated as ‘America’s best idea,’” Flyn writes. And it seems to have given rise to the contemporary concept of wilderness, which involves a region where “man himself is a visitor who does not remain.” It’s no coincidence that this concept has prevailed in nations where indigenous people have been displaced or massacred. In cases where the process of displacement was not complete prior to the creation of a national park, it often continued thereafter. It was not until 1969 (rather than 1929 as Flyn has it) that the last Indian village in Yosemite was burned down, and its inhabitants moved out of the park.

For all our efforts to create a wilderness in national parks, places like Yellowstone can leave the visitor feeling claustrophobic. Cars move bumper to bumper on the major roads, and Flyn feels that she is in a “Disneyfied wilderness,” with concession stands, toilet blocks, boardwalks, and interpretive signs. It’s a carefully managed experience: walking parties are precisely spaced, and each group removes all traces of their presence so that the next group, arriving a few hours later to see the hot springs, steam vents, and geysers, will feel like they are the only people in the area. Only when she gets a coveted permit to hike in the backcountry does she gain a sense of wilderness that chimes with her. Even when there are other hikers nearby, the solitude is, Flyn says, “an illusion worth protecting.”

The ultimate “wilderness” is surely Antarctica, and it is here that Flyn seems happiest. She joins a few dozen other tourists on a cruise, but keeps to herself, and is ecstatic when she is the only person on her motorboat to see a glacier front collapse. “It was just our secret, mine and the iceberg’s,” she writes. What she really wants from life, she decides, as she contemplates that empire of ice and silence, is a “quest without end.” As she stands on the deck of the ship, staring at the mist and ice, her hands and face numbing, she is transformed: “For a moment, my mind finally, finally, went still.”

Astonishingly, Flyn goes even further in her search for wilderness, to the bottom of the ocean. Her journey begins off the Bahamas, aboard a superyacht owned by a mega-millionaire who made a fortune in trash bags. Just a few weeks earlier the submersible Titan, en route to the wreck of the Titanic in the north Atlantic, had imploded, killing all five passengers. Flyn’s submersible takes her only to the floor of the shallow bay where the superyacht is anchored. Her accounts of the ocean’s depths come from others, some of whom have dived to the deepest point on Earth, the Challenger Deep in the western Pacific, around 11,000 meters below the surface.

In Nepal wilderness can also be sacred land. At Dolpo, a lama and his wife live by ancient laws in an “apparently wild landscape” far from the nearest village. Everything in and around Dolpo is owned by a zhibdak, a kind of local deity. If someone wishes to cut down a tree or remove stones from the river they must appeal to the zhibdak for permission. And they must never take more than they need, otherwise they will incur the wrath of the zhibdak: “Be careful, warned the lama. The gods are easily angered. One must be kind and respectful, thinking always of the whole.” Rare blue sheep visit the holy man on the fifteenth and thirtieth of every month, he tells Flyn; musk deer trek from the higher peaks to be in his company, and snow leopards come to his house.

Dolpo is now part of Nepal’s Shey Phoksundo National Park. People inhabit this park; Flyn observes that “destroying or disempowering” their belief systems “can disturb the equilibrium.” Indigenous people claim “rights over at least 38 million square kilometers of land, spread over six continents,” so the management model Flyn sees in Shey Phoksundo National Park is of potential global significance. But there is an enormous, inherent tension here. In 2022 a global environmental convention agreed to place 30 percent of land and waters worldwide under protection by 2030. Minority groups immediately condemned the initiative, fearing dispossession and disenfranchisement such as that seen in Uganda’s Virunga Mountains.

Credit is due to Flyn for her ambition. Countless erudite volumes have been devoted to the interactions of humans with their environment, the environmental impact of the interaction of colonial societies with indigenous cultures, and the effects of disparities of wealth on biodiversity. The discussion of wilderness is a jungle from which few return unscarred.

The Savage Landscape is a beautifully observed work of learning, pain, and disillusionment. Along the way we begin to understand Flyn as a person, and to better appreciate the motives that have driven so many, from hermits to zoologists like Fossey, to live alone in nature. But a more thorough exploration of the implications of various concepts of wilderness would have enriched her book. Moreover, its lack of a sense of deep history and of the impacts of climate change are major omissions that mar its attempts to understand the effects of such notions on biodiversity.

An often overlooked ecological problem with national parks “wildernesses” is that they suffer from the discontinuance of management by indigenous peoples. Nowhere is this more evident than in my country of Australia, where Aboriginal fire practices were so widespread and profound that they created the open, grassy landscape encountered by the first European settlers. Once those practices ceased, these landscapes swiftly transformed into dense forest. Today, places like Australia face immense challenges from fires of unprecedented scale and ferocity. Without human management, new, less diverse, and less sustainable environments will ensue.

entries.title: Reverence for All of It
entries.summary: Benedict de Spinoza’s ideas about the interchangeability of God and nature made him a heretic in seventeenth-century Europe. But would it be correct to call him an atheist today?
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
The seventeenth-century philosopher Benedict de Spinoza attracted a devoted circle of friends in his day, and now draws a wide and passionate readership. When people like Spinoza, they tend to really like him. I know this because I fell in love with his philosophy while studying it at university—it changed the way I saw the world—and now I receive emails from complete strangers telling me how much they love him too. His tendency to inspire devotion is all the more remarkable considering that his masterpiece, the Ethics, is a daunting work, written in a strict logical form modeled on Euclid’s Elements of Geometry.

Spinoza’s philosophical path began with an experience of anxiety, which he realized had been generated by socially constructed desires. “I saw that all the things which were the cause or object of my fear had nothing of good or bad in themselves, except insofar as [my] mind was moved by them,” he wrote around 1660, when he was in his late twenties. He had turned to philosophy—after a turbulent few years working in his family’s failing merchant business, getting into trouble with his Jewish community, and finding “ordinary life…empty and futile”—in search of “the true good.” Whatever this was, it would “continually give me the greatest joy, to eternity.” Spinoza lived in fractious times, and he came to believe that powerful negative emotions—hatred, envy, fear, shame, excessive desire for esteem—were the biggest obstacles to enlightenment. How can we live wisely and peacefully while conflicts rage all around us, and often inside of us too?

By all accounts, Spinoza—in both his writing and his daily life—made more progress than most on this question. Having left the hubbub of Amsterdam and turned down the flattering offer of a professorship in philosophy at the University of Heidelberg, he lived quietly while “his reputation flew everywhere.” He worked hard, grinding lenses to make a modest living while writing his Ethics, a short yet intricate book that took nine years to complete. Meanwhile, his polemical Theologico-Political Treatise, banned by the Vatican soon after it was published in 1670, circulated in false covers among Europe’s leading intellectuals. His landlady in The Hague, the last place he lived, thought her resident genius “very courteous and obliging”; according to Spinoza’s first biographer, she found his conversation “very sweet and easy…. He would very often discourse with…the people of the house, when they happened to be sick or afflicted; he never failed then to comfort them.” Though his habits were simple, they weren’t entirely austere: he enjoyed relaxing with “a pipe of tobacco.”

Spinoza’s metaphysical and psychological theories arose from a deep understanding of himself and others as expressions of an eternal, infinite reality. He famously called this reality “God or Nature”—a way of describing God that rejected the traditional religious idea of a creator separate from his creation. Spinoza argued that everything is “in God,” everything is “part of nature.” This yields a vision of ourselves not as substantial individuals who exist independently, as both Aristotle and Descartes thought, but as “finite modes”: transient, fluid forms expressing the power of “God or Nature” in singular ways. For Spinoza, human beings are less like little boats charting a course through choppy waters and more like ocean waves, metaphysically inseparable from the whole.

Many consequences follow from that radical thought. All our desires and actions flow necessarily from chains of previous events; free will, Spinoza argued, is an illusion. We believe that our choices are free and spontaneous only because we’re unaware of the causes that produced our desires. He criticized the Christian idea of sin and suggested that excessive humility is not a virtue but an unhelpful denigration of human nature. “We must always attend to those things which are good in each thing so that in this way we are always determined to acting from an affect of Joy,” he wrote in the Ethics.

For example, if someone sees that he pursues esteem too much, he should think of its correct use, the end for which it ought to be pursued, and the means by which it can be acquired, not of its misuse and emptiness, and men’s inconstancy, and other things of that kind, which only someone sick of mind thinks of.

Moralistic prohibitions on enjoyment—rather common in the Calvinist culture of his day—distorted true virtue, as he saw it. “Joy and Sadness,” he explained, “are passions by which each one’s power, or striving to persevere in his being, is increased or diminished.” So joy is what happens when the power of “God or Nature” surges and shines through us, and finds its fullest expression in our lives.

These insights seem to have lent Spinoza a quiet charisma. In the various places he lived in the Dutch Republic, he attracted friends and admirers. His dedicated inner circle (five or six men of various professions) gathered regularly in Amsterdam to read drafts of the Ethics and saw themselves as his disciples, according to a contemporary source. Yet Spinoza’s unorthodox views were condemned by both Catholic and Protestant churches, and he was deterred from publishing his Ethics because, as he wrote in 1675, “the Theologians were setting traps for me everywhere.” At some personal risk, his “disciples” worked together to publish the book in the months following his death in 1677.

One remarkable feature of the enduring enthusiasm for Spinoza’s philosophy is the wide spectrum of viewpoints it accommodates—especially on the question of religion. Somehow Romantic free spirits, observant Jews, Hindu nondualists, spiritual-but-not-religious seekers, Buddhists, hardline atheists, and Christians of different stripes have all taken inspiration from the Ethics. This broad appeal is not incidental. Spinoza lived in a time of extreme polarization, with Europe riven by the Thirty Years’ War and the Franco-Dutch War, among other conflicts. In this oppressive climate, he took great care to construct a radically inclusive philosophical vision that left room for people to interpret it according to their own religious loyalties. Spinoza wanted to bring many readers—“as many as possible,” he once wrote—along with him on his philosophical path. He argued for freedom and toleration in matters of belief, while shifting the very definition of religion onto more ethical terrain: whatever their opinions about priests or sacraments, surely everyone could agree on the values of justice and kindness?

Steven Nadler, a philosophy professor at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, has long been one of Spinoza’s most eloquent disciples. Not that Nadler himself would put it that way: his mission is to purge Spinoza’s philosophy of any religious connotations. A self-confessed “Spinoza fan,” he is the author of an excellent biography as well as several influential books on Spinoza’s ideas, always hailing him as a secular pioneer. Nadler’s new book doubles down on this interpretation, as its provocative title suggests: Spinoza, Atheist.

Many scholars have challenged the accusation—common among Spinoza’s earliest critics—that he was an atheist. Nowadays he is more often described as a pantheist or a panentheist: someone who retains a meaningful notion of God yet denies that this God is separate from nature as a whole. “Pantheism” literally means that everything is God, that God is everything; as Nadler explains, the word was coined by the Newtonian philosopher Joseph Raphson in 1697 to describe philosophies (including Spinoza’s) that “posit a certain universal substance, both material and also intelligent, forming all things.” “Panentheism,” a term the Spinozist philosopher Friedrich Schelling invented in 1809, suggests that God contains the world, a view closer to traditional theism, since it allows for the possibility that God exceeds the world in some way. Panentheism means that everything is in God.

On the face of it, this is exactly what Spinoza himself wrote. One of the most important propositions in the Ethics states that “whatever is, is in God, and nothing can be or be conceived without God.” Far from denying God’s existence, Spinoza argued—in accord with many theologians—that existence belongs to God’s very essence: in some sense, “God or Nature” is existence itself. The question that sets Spinoza apart from orthodoxy is whether this God causes finite things to exist outside himself (the standard view) or within himself, as ephemeral “modifications” or expressions of his own eternal being (Spinoza’s view, summed up in his claim that “God is the immanent, not the transitive, cause of all things”).

The Ethics is filled with references to God, and culminates in the statement that “Blessedness consists in Love of God.” Nonetheless, Nadler makes a brilliant case for Spinoza’s atheism, bringing new analytical depth to the views he advocated in his previous books. He also tells a great story. Although ideas take center stage in Spinoza, Atheist, Nadler manages to keep even well-informed readers in a state of intellectual suspense. His book treats Spinoza’s religious position not just as a matter of interpretation or a point for scholarly debate, but as a mystery to be solved.

Instead of going straight to Spinoza’s texts to unravel this mystery, Nadler amps up the drama by beginning with the rumors and accusations that swirled around the philosopher in the seventeenth century. He starts with Pierre Bayle’s widely read Historical and Critical Dictionary, first published in 1697, twenty years after Spinoza’s death. Bayle’s gossipy “profile” of Spinoza (as Nadler aptly calls it) is the longest entry in this vast multivolume work. Bayle goes into some detail about the philosopher’s background—his parents were Portuguese Jews whose families had fled the Inquisition and settled in Amsterdam—before recounting Spinoza’s permanent expulsion from the Jewish community there in 1656, at the age of twenty-three, for teaching “horrifying heresies.”

Those unorthodox views did not fare any better with Christian authorities. In the Theologico-Political Treatise, as Bayle notes, Spinoza questioned the truth of the Jewish and Christian scriptures. He disliked the Jews’ claim to be God’s chosen people and the Christians’ insistence that everyone should share their beliefs; in other words, he denounced both Jewish particularism and Christian universalism. Spinoza also scorned belief in so-called miracles—a bedrock of Christian faith and, perhaps more to the point, of ecclesial power—as ignorance dressed up as devotion.

Turning to the more metaphysical Ethics, Bayle declares himself appalled by the “horrible idea” that “God is the only substance that there is in the universe, and that all other beings are only modifications of that substance.” Bayle likens Spinoza’s all-encompassing God to the “very current” Hindu doctrine—then circulating in Europe, thanks to reports by missionaries returning from India—that God is “like an immense ocean” in which all individual things are submerged, “united to their whole.” Although Bayle doesn’t mean this as a compliment, the comparison between Spinozist and Hindu nondualism persisted for more than three centuries, as Westerners came to regard both philosophies in a much more positive light. And Bayle’s oceanic analogy has proved rather handy to explain Spinoza’s view of the relationship between God and all the particular, finite things that are “in God.”

According to Bayle, this idea was “monstrous.” Nadler explains that Bayle was most disturbed by its moral consequences: a God so implicated in the world must be “responsible for the most immoral thoughts and heinous crimes committed by human beings.” Like many other contemporaries and near-contemporaries, Bayle did not just disapprove of Spinoza’s philosophy but feared it—perhaps because its relentless rationality was so powerful, so difficult to refute. There seems to be a glimmer of ambivalence in Bayle’s judgment of Spinoza as “the greatest atheist who ever lived.”

As Bayle’s comparison between Spinozism and Hinduism suggests, in the seventeenth century “atheist” did not mean what it typically means today: someone who denies God’s existence. Nadler’s first two chapters provide illuminating historical detail on this point, showing how the highly “ambiguous” word was applied to anyone who deviated from Christian orthodoxy. In Spinoza’s Holland, the established Reformed Church condemned unconventional sects, including Quakers and Anabaptists, as atheist. More loosely still, the charge of atheism could encompass libertine lifestyles and questionable morals. As Nadler notes, “atheist” was “an all-purpose pejorative,” with an elasticity similar to that of “Communist” in twentieth-century America. Most philosophers in the 1600s were accused of atheism at some point—even Malebranche, a Catholic priest.

This means that contemporary critics such as Bayle (and numerous others) were correct, or at least consistent, in calling Spinoza an atheist. Yet it also means that those accusations of atheism don’t tell us much about whether Spinoza was an atheist in the sense that we now understand the term.

Before he addresses this question by turning to Spinoza’s own writings, Nadler traces the spectacular transformation of Spinoza’s reputation. By 1700 “Spinozist” and “atheist” were practically synonyms; Spinoza appeared to have been well and truly canceled. Within a hundred years, however—thanks in part to the open-mindedness of Goethe and the German Romantics, in part to the gradual decline of ecclesial influence over intellectual life—he had transitioned from heretic to hero. In 1785 Goethe warmly endorsed his view that “Being is God”: “And if for this reason others scold Spinoza for being an atheist,” Goethe wrote, “I should like to name him and praise him as theissimum [most theistic].” Gripped by “Spinoza fever,” a new generation of free-thinking poets and philosophers—including Novalis, Feuerbach, Coleridge, Emerson, George Eliot—turned to Spinozism as an alternative spirituality. This non-Christian philosophy made it possible to see manifestations of divine power throughout nature, in multiple incarnations, and especially in human creativity.

Nadler concedes that there is something to this interpretation, still popular among both scholars and nonspecialists. Spinoza’s rejection of a personal God with plans and preferences, his refusal to separate God from nature, and the consequence that “God or Nature” is indiscriminately the cause of pleasure and pain, virtue and vice, are all features of pantheism. And yet, argues Nadler, pantheism involves a religious attitude that is missing from Spinoza’s thought. Practicing pantheists regard “God or Nature” as an object of wonder and awe, devotion and worship. Practicing Spinozists, by contrast, are just doing philosophy: seeking to understand themselves as part of nature, or, in Nadler’s words, “obtaining the most perfect knowledge of things in the world around us”—a description that embraces scientific as well as philosophical inquiry. Spinoza’s God, he emphasizes, lacks “anything remotely moral or value-laden. God is not good, wise, just, righteous, or benevolent.” So why call it “God” at all?

These points—all of them well argued—lay the ground for Nadler’s penultimate chapter, titled “Spinoza’s Atheism.” Here he distinguishes between the metaphysical aspect of atheism and its “psychological or spiritual” aspect. Metaphysically, atheism and pantheism are identical: they “essentially agree on what there is…. There is only Nature,” nothing supernatural. Psychologically, however, they are very different. Pantheism is “still a ‘theism’” as long as its practitioners treat nature with “reverence, worshipful awe, or some other religious mindset appropriate to a divinity.” And although Spinoza’s “Nature” resembles God in being the eternal and infinite source of all that exists, there is still “nothing holy or sacred or ineffable about Nature…. there is no ‘cult’ or ‘religion’ of nature.” Nor, Nadler adds, does Spinoza’s philosophy mandate “any kind of humbling of self.”

These insights add up to a convincing case that a Spinozist need not be a pantheist, and can be an atheist, based on Nadler’s “psychological” definition of these terms. I am not so sure it follows that a Spinozist cannot be a pantheist and must be an atheist. While Spinoza does not extol nature-worship, he nowhere prohibits it. Indeed, his attitude to religious practice was a principled tolerance. His criticisms of certain Jewish and Christian practices were made at a time when people were reprimanded, excommunicated, or even persecuted for not following those practices, and do not necessarily translate into a blanket condemnation of religious pursuits within a more liberal and less fearmongering milieu. Spinoza urged the family with whom he lodged in The Hague to attend church regularly, and occasionally went himself to hear a certain Lutheran preacher whose sermons he admired.

The pantheist camp (let’s picture them gathered around a fire in the woods) might also protest that awe, wonder, and reverence are not the only religious attitudes available. What about feeling at peace because everything must be exactly as it is, as Spinoza’s determinism entails? Or expressing gratitude for being alive—gratitude that might be directed not toward a creator God, but to the infinite causes that sustain each unique life? When the Romantic theologian Friedrich Schleiermacher described religious emotion as, in essence, a “feeling of absolute dependence,” he was expressing a Spinozist sentiment. Similarly, Spinoza’s metaphysics invites us to see ourselves as parts of an eternal, infinite whole, which is just the sort of cosmic connectedness cited by people who might describe themselves as “spiritual but not religious.” Devotion to nature can be expressed in many ways: by ethical action (including ecological activism), by contemplation, by making art, by doing math, by scientific inquiry, or by rituals of celebration and thanksgiving. Spinoza was a rationalist, but he was not a puritan. “It is the part of a wise man,” he wrote in the Ethics,

to refresh and restore himself in moderation with pleasant food and drink, with scents, with the beauty of green plants, with decoration, music, sports, the theater, and other things of this kind, which anyone can use without injury to another.

Why not sing and dance around the campfire?

By showing that the real difference between atheism and pantheism is psychological—a matter of one’s attitude toward “God or Nature”—Nadler moves the Spinoza conversation onto surprising new ground. Although he began by asking whether Spinozism is atheism or pantheism, by the end of the book that question seems less pressing, and even somewhat misplaced. In the original Latin, Spinoza’s celebrated phrase “God or Nature” is Deus sive natura, and sive is an inclusive “or” that means something like “i.e.,” or “in other words.” (The other word that Spinoza might have used is aut, a disjunctive “or” that names alternatives, as in, “Do you want tea or coffee?”) For Spinoza, “God or Nature” doesn’t offer a choice between two different things so much as an elaboration and expansion of possibilities. The phrase cleverly leaves it open, so that many people can take up his philosophy, as Spinoza himself hoped.

Nadler’s book testifies to the fact that atheists today can “recognize Spinoza as a fellow traveler.” This is true, in my view, because Spinoza was not traveling toward any particular religious (or irreligious) destination. His philosophy seeks instead a deeper understanding of human beings and their flourishing. To that end, it is crucial to be allowed to think freely, unencumbered by religious dogma. We all share the capacity to reason: to see that 2+2=4, and to make inferences about cause and effect. Alongside this, though, Spinoza emphasized that we also share the capacity to attend to our own thoughts and feelings, and to perceive them more clearly: “Each of us has—in part, at least, if not absolutely—the power to understand himself and his affects [i.e., his emotions], and consequently, the power to bring it about that he is less acted on by them.” And he knew “by experience” that we all struggle to exercise those capacities whenever we are swayed by powerful desires or anxieties, or find ourselves in stressful circumstances; all too often, to quote Ovid, “we see the better and approve it, but follow the worse.”

So Spinoza advised his readers not only to cultivate their rational powers, but also to pay attention to their own fluctuating emotions. The Ethics is a five-part book: the first part focuses on God, the second examines the human mind, and the remaining three are all about emotions and how to deal with them. These subjects are intimately connected because, in Spinoza’s view, “hate, anger, envy, etc., follow from the same necessity” as every other expression of “God or Nature.” He studied human passions with the logical rigor and objectivity with which Euclid studied geometry, analyzing each emotion “just as if it were a Question of lines, planes and bodies.” And as in mathematics, this method can deliver clarity without shirking complexity. Take, for example, this cool specification of ambivalence:

If someone imagines that a thing he loves is united with another by as close, or by a closer, bond of Friendship than that with which he himself, alone, possessed the thing, he will be affected with Hate toward the thing he loves, and will envy the other.

Furthermore:

If someone begins to hate a thing he has loved, so that the Love is completely destroyed, then (from an equal cause) he will have a greater hate for it than if he had never loved it, and this hate will be the greater as the Love before was greater.

Reading the Ethics, one is liable to feel seen. If so, the text is having its desired effect. One aim of Spinoza’s emotional geometry is to cut through the stories we weave around our upsets and triumphs, and hold up a mirror to the thing itself: this is envy, this is sadness, this is wonder, and so on. And of course, when we come to know our own all-too-human being in this way, we’re becoming better acquainted with “God or Nature.”

It is fun to debate different interpretations of a text as rich as the Ethics, especially in the company of such an erudite and stylish writer as Steven Nadler. Spinoza, Atheist is a model of courteous disagreement. Without getting lost in scholarly minutiae, Nadler brings dissenting voices to the page and gives them fair hearing. He is also prepared to question himself; at one point he wonders whether trying to settle the question of Spinoza’s atheism is a “fool’s errand.” He takes seriously the objection that squeezing such an original philosophical system into a ready-made category, whether atheism or pantheism, is unlikely to do it justice.

Having banged the pantheist drum myself in the past—I love a nature retreat and a solstice party—I closed this book with the realization that insisting on any one label is at odds with the inclusive spirit of Spinozism. The “atheist” label, in particular, runs the further risk of blunting the radical edge of Spinoza’s thinking—which Nadler brings out so eloquently—and thereby diminishing its enduring significance. If Spinoza were simply an atheist in the modern sense, that would make him ahead of his time in the seventeenth century, but not especially interesting today when atheism is so common and, in some settings, the mainstream view.

But as Nadler makes plain, even if Spinozism can be atheism, it is not merely a flat denial of God’s existence that leaves modern secular life unquestioned. On the contrary, this metaphysical vision is gloriously counterintuitive. “What is a philosopher like Spinoza doing,” asks Nadler, “if not trying to get us to rethink the way we look at the world, to reorient our empirical perception of things?” Most of all, Spinoza was getting us to look anew at our own interconnected lives, instead of relying on religious or political dogmas to tell us who we are and how to live. “Most people, I believe, do not know themselves,” he wrote. “Fear makes them turn this way and that”—and others can exploit that uncertainty to their own advantage. He warned that his philosophical path wouldn’t always be easy. “All things excellent are as difficult as they are rare,” he writes at the end of the Ethics. And yet, he urges, “salvation” is within our power: we all possess the resources to find out what makes us feel sad and anxious, and what brings lasting joy and peace. This effort of self-understanding always was, and still is, the beating heart of Spinozism.

entries.title: Masters of Their Craft
entries.summary: For 150 years Paris was the research hub, testing ground, and production center for modern painting and sculpture.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
Paris, a city of museums, outdid itself this past summer, with enormous exhibitions devoted to Michelangelo’s influence on Rodin, Renoir’s drawings and paintings, the final dozen years of Matisse’s life, and Calder’s mobiles and stabiles. Each one had its own story to tell. But the shows also overlapped and became part of a larger story about the 150 years when Paris was the research hub, testing ground, engine room, and production center for modern painting and sculpture.

Could it be that the radically divergent achievements of Rodin, Renoir, Matisse, and Calder share some common attitude or approach? I think they do. The beginning of an answer can be found in something Rilke wrote about Rodin, whom he served as a secretary for a year or so: “His art was not built upon a great idea, but upon a minute, conscientious realization, upon the attainable, upon a craft.” When Rilke spoke of craft it wasn’t in the limited technical sense of how an artist manipulates plaster or makes a cast in bronze; he was referring to Rodin’s thoroughgoing engagement with the building blocks of the visual arts. That involved a close observation of nature and a tireless examination of the surface of the human body—what Rilke called “this differently great surface, variedly accentuated, accurately measured, out of which everything must rise.” It wasn’t that artists in Paris didn’t have feelings and opinions about nationalism, socialism, a resurgent Catholicism, or any number of other political and social developments. They were affected by all of this, as they were by the revolutions of 1848, the Franco-Prussian War, the Paris Commune, the Great Depression, and two world wars. But through it all, from Ingres, Delacroix, Corot, and Courbet in the mid-nineteenth century to Matisse, Picasso, Braque, Giacometti, and Balthus a century later, questions of craft remained the essential questions.

Matisse could be a Baudelairean when he thought about women and almost a Catholic when he conceived the Chapel of the Rosary at Vence. He could be a realist and an abstractionist, a romantic and a classicist. He could be all these things because before all else he was an artist with an exacting eye and a brilliant hand, working with paint, ink, brushes, and pencils—and ultimately, when he turned to cut paper, a pair of scissors. The meaning began with the mystery of the making. Ideas mattered. But ideas, however strongly held and passionately argued, could only persuade if the artist was a master of his craft. As Rilke wrote of Rodin, “He was a worker whose only desire was to penetrate with all his forces into the humble and difficult significance of his tools.” Craft was the crux of the matter. This was the Parisian ethic, whether an artist was born there, as Rodin was, or somewhere else in France, like Renoir and Matisse, or somewhere else entirely, as with Calder, who was painting cityscapes when he arrived in Paris from New York in 1926 and became an abstract sculptor four years later.

I know I’m not the only person who worried that “Michelangelo Rodin: Living Bodies” at the Louvre was going to be a potboiler, a clash of titans engineered to appeal to the largest imaginable audience. Whatever the show’s mass appeal, what I found was as searching an exploration of artistic influence as I’ve ever encountered in a museum. I saw—and I could see that others saw—how all the knowledge of a sixteenth-century Italian immersed in Catholic theology, Neoplatonic thought, and homoerotic desire was absorbed by a nineteenth-century bohemian whose world had been shaped by Nietzsche, Wagner, and the cult of the femme fatale. What linked these two utterly different men—it was demonstrated in every gallery—were fundamental matters of sculptural craft, how specific muscular movements, by opening and activating space, generated a kinetic energy and a pictorial drama. Out of the most particular shared formal strategies emerged radically different kinds of meaning.

Near the beginning of the show there was a gallery highlighting the presence of works by Michelangelo in Paris in the nineteenth century: both originals, especially the Slaves in the Louvre, and plaster casts and replicas, many at the École des Beaux-Arts on the Left Bank (see illustration at top of article). Rodin wasn’t the only artist who was interested; the show included drawings after Michelangelo by Degas and Cézanne. What seems to have particularly fascinated Rodin were Michelangelo’s figures of Night, Day, Dawn, and Dusk in the Medici tombs in Florence. Michelangelo’s figures, especially the women with their unnaturally massive, rather masculine musculature, were allegorical, their restlessness not psychological but cosmological. In 1877 Rodin made some drawings after those enigmatic beings, rather straightforward studies in a soft charcoal, emphasizing how Michelangelo, by joining the torso, pelvis, and legs in a spiraling arabesque, gave dynamism to inherently static reclining poses.

In the Louvre show, Rodin’s 1877 studies of the female Night and Dawn were hung near several drawings he did decades later, between 1910 and 1913, in which the cosmic power of Michelangelo’s torqued pelvis and thighs was suddenly earthbound, reimagined as outrageous fin-de-siècle eroticism. As Rodin drew a dancer, Alda Moreno, her thighs were opening—awakening—to welcome a sexual partner. The torsions in Rodin’s new drawings were very close to the ones he’d observed in Michelangelo’s Night and Dawn; it was the meanings that were radically different. Rodin was aware of what he was doing. We know that because one of his drawings bears a scrawled, enigmatic inscription: “pendant M A [Michel-Ange] a lautre Moreno.” Apparently Rodin liked that Alda Moreno’s initials were the same as Michelangelo’s, only in reverse.

Everywhere in this show, which included some three dozen Michelangelo drawings, I felt the formal challenges that united these two artists from different times and places, even as they pursued their own imaginative ends. In one remarkable section some of the fragments of bodies and body parts that are still gathered in Rodin’s studio were juxtaposed with Michelangelo’s drawings of a thigh, a knee, a shoulder, a foot. What both artists were looking for in the dynamics of bone, sinew, and muscle were expressive building blocks, the elements that when taken together give the human figure a mobility that generates psychological and even moral power. That same kind of thinking, on a much grander scale, united Michelangelo’s Moses (seen in a copy) and Rodin’s Balzac (in an original plaster). At the Louvre Moses and Balzac made a pair as riveting as it was unexpected. The prophetic authority of Michelangelo’s enormous figure, whom Catholics regard as a founder of the Judeo-Christian tradition, was echoed in the figure of the megalomaniacal nineteenth-century novelist, the supreme chronicler of the chaotic secular life of Paris. I realized at the Louvre that Rodin had discovered in Michelangelo—or at least found himself concurring with Michelangelo—that a massive volume could suggest an ethical imperative. By somehow simultaneously declaring and defying the inevitability of gravity, the heroic figure, although earthbound, achieves a visionary intensity, tragic and divine.

In recent years art historians who’ve taken an interest in eighteenth- and nineteenth-century Paris have generally focused on the city as social spectacle. That was certainly a preoccupation among the artists, from Watteau in the early eighteenth century, when he painted Gersaint’s Shopsign (1721), with its novelistic impressions of the interior of a picture dealer’s premises, through Courbet’s The Artist’s Studio (1854–1855), and Manet’s A Bar at the Folies-Bergère (1882), down to two of Renoir’s masterpieces, Dance at the Moulin de la Galette (1876) and Luncheon of the Boating Party (1880–1881), both included in “Renoir and Love,” which along with “Renoir’s Drawings” made a doubleheader at the Musée d’Orsay. Rodin was an important figure in nineteenth-century Parisian society, among the artists Henry James would have had in mind when he dreamed up the sculptor Gloriani, in whose home Lambert Strether, the protagonist of The Ambassadors, has his revelation about the need to “live all you can; it’s a mistake not to.” But the Louvre exhibition suggested that as much as Paris was for artists a place to see and be seen, it was even more important as a city of museums, exhibitions, art schools, and studios—a place to test the strengths, weaknesses, possibilities, and limitations of one’s craft. For artists Paris was, whatever the city’s glamour and romance, an ideal place to do their work, to live the life of art most intensely, day by day, hour by hour.

Before artists were dreamers, they were workers. That’s why Diderot, a writer who understood the struggles of the creative life, opened his Salon of 1765, the book that by many measures marks the beginning of modern art and modern art criticism, with a long excerpt from a speech by Chardin, probably the greatest of all still life painters, about the education of the artist. This, Diderot insisted, was where everything had to begin. Chardin described the trials any young artist went through in order to master the craft, after which, as he put it, “we turn to the resources of our own genius, if we have any.” Before discussing the works in the Salon, Diderot emphasized exactly how they were made, with “paint and brush in painting, chalk in drawing, chisel and clay in sculpture, burin, stone, and metal in printmaking, bow-drill in precious stone carving.” While he filled his pages with detailed descriptions and analyses of the narratives that preoccupied so many eighteenth-century artists—Greuze one of his favorites among them—he chose to return to the question of craft at the end of the book in an appendix entitled “Notes on Painting,” which began with his thoughts about drawing, color, and chiaroscuro. A straight line can be traced from Diderot to Rilke’s insistence on Rodin’s fascination with “the humble and difficult significance of his tools.”
