If for Rodin craft meant reimagining the human figure with “new surfaces, new gestures” that almost inevitably echoed Michelangelo’s older ones, for Renoir the key to everything was Venetian color and composition, the heritage of Titian and Veronese. An argument can be made that much of Renoir’s career involved an ongoing encounter with Veronese’s The Wedding at Cana (1563), the immense canvas that throughout the nineteenth century was a major attraction at the Louvre—and still is today. Never have I experienced a drawing show where I felt as strongly as in “Renoir Drawings” that the graphic arts are a prelude to painting, the relatively discrete strokes of pastel a preparation for the seductions of oil paint. In Renoir’s drawings you see the workmanlike construction that undergirds his delicious flights of fancy. He’s right up there with Chardin and Degas as he lays down pastel strokes in complementary, contrapuntal strokes of red and green or orange and blue that echo the dissonant harmonies of the Venetian Renaissance. In The Loge (1874), Pinning the Hat (1890), and Child with an Apple (circa 1895), color is becoming flesh, the process perhaps not quite so complete as in some of the paintings, yet with a rawness that has its own fascination. While these pastels reveal a Renoir who’s aligning himself with the Romanticism of Delacroix, when he works in graphite or red and white chalk he’s obviously thinking about the methods of Ingres and the classicists; his experiments are grounded not in Venetian colorito but in Florentine disegno, the figure’s circumscribing contour the essential thing. But even many of the chalk studies that seem to begin with a contour eventually become vigorously volumetric, the linear intelligence sensualized in extraordinary large drawings, including Study for “La Coiffure” (1900–1901), which was owned by Picasso, a great admirer of his.

Renoir was a hard worker and a hedonist. Without the hard work—it’s there in every one of his astonishing drawings—the hedonism would be kitsch. His ravishing Dance at the Moulin de la Galette is a searching exploration of the chaotic exuberance of youthful love and friendship, the sentiment (not sentimentality) enlarged through the monumental coloristic orchestrations he had studied in The Wedding at Cana. Five years later, in Luncheon of the Boating Party, the informality of the composition, with young men and women turning this way and that, is again both confirmed and complicated by the exactitude of his technique. Renoir is a brilliant storyteller—the young woman almost kissing the little dog is one of the great images in European painting—but he never lets us forget that the storytelling begins with the paint and the brush, the dancing strokes of black and white, the expanses of red and green, the punctuation of two yellow straw hats (one on a young man, the other on the young woman with the dog). The long history of painterly painting, going back to Pompeii and including not only Titian and Veronese but also Rubens, Van Dyck, and Watteau, informs Renoir’s celebration of bohemian life in the early years of the Third Republic.

In nineteenth- and twentieth-century Paris, artists regarded visual culture as universal culture. The lessons of far-flung times, places, and artists were assimilated not as history, sociology, or anthropology but as technical and formal problems to be solved in the studio. The result—on full display in “Matisse: 1941–1954” at the Grand Palais—was that meanings and metaphors were sharpened, the allusions to anything from Renaissance compositions to Byzantine icons to Islamic patterns grounded not in superficial quotations but in formal and structural explorations. The Grand Palais covered much of the same ground as the tremendous exhibition devoted to Matisse’s paper cutouts at the Museum of Modern Art in New York a decade ago, but by including the full range of his work in his later years—not only cutouts but also paintings, drawings, illustrated books, and some of his innumerable studies for the Vence chapel—the Parisian show revealed an even more complex artist: restless, endlessly curious, determined to move in multiple directions.

The Matisse that museumgoers encountered at the Grand Palais wasn’t so much a genius as a genius-craftsman. The cut-paper compositions that increasingly preoccupied him beginning in the early 1940s and eventually reached mural-scale dimensions couldn’t alone satisfy his continuing desire to see what he could do with a range of media, including pen and pencil, brush and ink, oil paint, linocut, lithography, and even stained glass. The figures he cut out of sheets of blue paper were like nothing anybody had ever seen, but so were the heraldic faces he drew with a thick brush dipped in ink around the same time, in 1952. And oil painting continued to hold his attention.

I’d never seen so many of the late paintings in one place—I’m not sure this many have been gathered together before—and as much as the late cutouts suggested a longing for an entirely new kind of pictorial art, the oil paintings suggested that Matisse was still eager to confront some rather old-fashioned challenges. I was especially glad to see a few canvases from a group made in 1947, with two women seated at a table before an enormous window. In a sense they’re genre paintings—you could imagine Vermeer or De Hooch embracing the motif—but the calligraphic paint handling and hyperbolic color tell their own story. For all their bravura they’re also modest paintings.

In the works at the Grand Palais Matisse could certainly be bold, but at times he was also almost hesitant, struggling to master something new or unfamiliar. In his last decade this artist who had probably always believed that art was an apprenticeship was still seeing what more he could do with the tools immediately at hand, letting them take the lead. Is it any wonder that for a brief time, more than three decades earlier, he had run an art school in Paris? The fundamentals that Matisse believed in were artisanal rather than philosophical. As long as you were learning how to handle a brush loaded with oil paint you were free to think whatever you wanted.

The language of the studio was a common language—a universal language. And in Paris artists from different places were welcome to shape it in very different ways. That’s why it was in Paris that Mondrian became most Dutch, Brancusi most Romanian, Picasso most Spanish, Chagall most Russian, and Calder, the subject of an immense show at the Fondation Louis Vuitton, most American. When Calder, who came to Paris as a young man, began making abstract sculpture in the early 1930s, his friend Léger observed in the introduction to a catalog that although Calder was 100 percent American and some of the artists with whom he shared a taste for the “transparent, objective, exact” were 100 percent French, somehow they all managed to “meet.” They were Americans and Europeans, but before everything else they were artists.

Calder spent much of his life in France, first in the late 1920s and early 1930s and then for decades after World War II, and the work in the beautifully organized retrospective at the Fondation Louis Vuitton was certainly part of the larger Parisian story. The first series of sculptures Calder made in France, the studies in wire of dancers, performers, athletes, and some of his artist friends, was a response to the Parisian spectacle, and in that sense not entirely unrelated to Renoir’s ambitions when he painted Dance at the Moulin de la Galette and Luncheon of the Boating Party. Calder’s wire portraits of Josephine Baker captured the champagne high of the 1920s, the period the French call les années folles. Before I saw the Calder retrospective, I worried that the Fondation Louis Vuitton, one of those Frank Gehry buildings in which a brilliant architect risks self-parody, might overwhelm the subtle muscularity of Calder’s mobiles and stabiles. But inside the galleries Calder was in full control, the relatively large spaces offering all the light and air that his slender, eloquently shaped volumes needed to move and expand with a serene monumentality—a laidback pageantry—that confounded the work’s actual dimensions.

The relaxed pacing of the show echoed the elegant rhythms of Calder’s greatest mobiles. And it was a pleasure to see a few of his works juxtaposed with paintings by Parisian friends, including Mondrian, Léger, Miró, and Hélion. Calder was part of a generation of Parisian artists who were explorers and discoverers, the first to see art in the abstract, their work grounded not in direct observation of nature but in the building blocks of nature: physical forces, biological processes, geometric forms. At the beginning of the 1930s Calder grasped those new possibilities as clearly as anybody, now using the wire lines, circles, curves, and arabesques with which he’d already created men, women, and animals to invent abstractions of a Platonic purity. They’re among the most austere works of his long career, and coming after the dancers and athletes with their années folles swagger, they reveal Calder digging even deeper into the spirit of Paris (see illustration on right). The craftsman is now a magician making something out of virtually nothing, some aspect of eternity suggested with a few pieces of curving wire. Is it any wonder that despite the reputation that Calder began building in the United States in the late 1930s—he had a major exhibition at the Museum of Modern Art in 1943—the greatest pages ever written about his work are by Sartre, who saw the meandering mobiles through the eyes of a Parisian existentialist? In postwar Europe Calder found an audience that grasped the metaphysical implications of his balancing acts.

Calder liked to refer to the place where he worked not as a studio but as a workshop. He said it as an American who rejected the aestheticism of the old European ateliers. But he was also affirming the absolutely artisanal nature of art—and that was an essential Parisian attitude. To regard oneself as a worker rather than an artist was a way of simplifying things, making sure that you never lost track of the basics. What drew so many artists to Paris was an awareness that in Paris being an artist was the most natural thing in the world. In 1880, when Henry James, that acute analyst of transatlantic culture, wrote a long essay about Delacroix’s letters, he left no doubt about the privileged place artists held:

In France the artist finds himself, ex officio, a member of a large and various society of fellow-workers; whatever may be his individual value, his basis or platform is a large and solid one, resting upon social position and social opinion. He has to make his work a success, but he has not…to justify and defend his point of view.

If Calder sometimes felt more comfortable in France than in the United States, it may have been because in the United States the artist was regarded as an outsider and an oddball. Even the artists Americans eventually embraced—I’m thinking of Hopper and Pollock—were never regarded as quite fitting in. They were alien, renegades in one way or another.

As an American visiting Paris, I’m always aware that I run the risk of romanticizing the place of artists, exhibitions, and museums in a culture I can’t help but view from a distance. But I don’t think I’m entirely mistaken in believing that even the exhilaration of a great exhibition feels a little different in Paris than it does in New York. In New York a powerful Renoir, Matisse, or Calder show can be a shock to the system, whereas in Paris it’s something to be taken in stride. If I’m right about this, then the explanation must be found in James’s observations about the place of artists as “fellow-workers” in the Parisian social world. In Paris the artist isn’t a paradoxical figure but an inevitable one. Going to see art in Paris, we may expect that we’re going to be seeing the loftiest achievements presented in the loftiest places. But what held me over the summer as I went from one astonishing exhibition to the next was the matter-of-factness of it all. What I was seeing were workers doing their work. Even the greatest masterpieces have matter-of-fact beginnings.

entries.content:
I like James Bond movies because you

Can hear punches land before they land.

The punch line reads: Today an oddity,

Tomorrow a standard. The material

I appropriate is available to anyone

Who cares to use it. The fact that

The material has been observed

By persons other than me defines

Its desires and threats on the spot.

It’s not like you have to wait for

Some water to fall on the heart.

Then wait for it to evaporate.

Then wait for the cool to remain.

Getting it takes only five seconds.

Some see leaves falling from a tree

And see it as leaves falling from a tree.

Two gods are better than one. Forget

How to swim or ride a bicycle or fly

An airplane if you can even dare to try.

I want to see it coming. I want to be

Shot in the dark with tracers. I live

Inside a bracing pornographic novel,

Long abandoned but still emblematic

Of the one true form of freedom in

That it tries to deal with how we use

And exploit each other in the most

Urgent and familiar ways imaginable.

A psychopath never goes out of style.

entries.content:
I dreamt we were like two wax birds, dreamt

we were a modest kitchen painted in red

gas or pink formaldehyde, dreamt you

were a convex shape that could contain all

of Rome or the one-light town where you were

born, a western sunset painted on a wooden

cross, my palms outstretched to reveal

the small skeleton of a winter tern, a roach, jade stone

cheap charm bracelet filled with teeth, “milk bones”

the fluid morning asters they call in this gray light

mourning doves, an old film projecting

its waning stream behind the refrigerator door,

tiny flight of light where we could see all

fourteen stages of the cross played by a misty-eyed

John Prine, my fingers unlacing in a liver-yellow

wind, missing my father most of all, missing

your silver-bellied goats which all fled

earlier that day through the radio, a tarmac hole

in the rosy mountain theme-park wall.

entries.title: The Executioner’s Song
entries.summary: Pamela Colloff's To Catch the Devil is as much the tale of a notorious jailhouse informant who put an innocent man on death row as it is the story of the officials and institutions that encouraged his lies.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
This past June, Jim Dailey’s eightieth birthday brought with it a gruesome distinction: if Florida manages to kill him, he will become one of the few octogenarians ever executed in the US. He knows that, absent some miracle, he will die alone, but he cannot say for certain whether death will come at the hands of the state or by the workings of his own body. In the nearly forty years he has spent on death row, Dailey has watched 125 other condemned men and two women go to the execution chambers in Florida, including, in July, two senior citizens put to death on the same day. Over that same four-decade period, some three hundred other Floridians have died waiting for the state to kill them. This is the more common end for an American on death row in the twenty-first century; in Louisiana last year, an eighty-one-year-old man died of natural causes—as much as any cause can be said to be natural after decades of isolation, poor medical care, and prison food—a mere three weeks before his scheduled execution.

Dailey is on death row today because he had the misfortune of being briefly held in the same county lockup as Paul Skalnik, one of the country’s most prolific jailhouse informants—a man so outrageous it is hard to accept he is not the product of a rather wild imagination. In fact he has been reconstructed meticulously by the investigative journalist Pamela Colloff for her first book, Catch the Devil. Skalnik is a rogue, an inveterate fabulist who trades in sleek cars and room service and ersatz diamond rings, a con man who sees the people around him as putty to be molded as he wishes. He has accumulated as many aliases and fabricated backstories—lawyer, Southwest Airlines executive, college football star, decorated Vietnam vet—as he has purple felt pouches, squirreled away every time he buys a new bottle of Crown Royal. “He was the hero of every story,” Colloff writes: a delusional showboat who, at one point, fibbing about interest from New York publishers in his manuscript, expressed regret that a (fictional) prospective advance wouldn’t equal Hillary Clinton’s. Over the decades, he married nine different women, sometimes without bothering to divorce the previous wife. His most cherished hobbies include writing bad checks and bilking single moms and widows out of their life savings.

In short, Skalnik is a habitual criminal who will say anything if he stands to gain, and thus a perfect jailhouse snitch. In the nine years preceding his fateful encounter with Dailey, his testimony sent some twenty-seven men in Pinellas County to prison—three of them to death row. In criminal cases, in which certainty is often elusive, Skalnik’s input nudged jurors past the line of reasonable doubt, turning even a weak case into a win. Not all the men he accused were innocent, but his lies moved their crimes into another echelon:

He was the state’s closer, the witness whose words moved jurors to choose death. Where there was room for doubt, Skalnik erased it, as he did in [Kenneth] Gardner’s case, when his testimony put the murder weapon in Gardner’s hands. Where jurors might consider leniency, as in [Richard] Cooper’s case, Skalnik told a story to harden their hearts. Cooper was still a teenager and looked even younger than his age—a potentially mitigating fact that could have earned the jury’s mercy, until Skalnik turned it against him. “He said no jury would ever sentence him to the death chair,” Skalnik testified, “because he’s nineteen years old and because he’s got that little baby face.”

In the mid-1980s a “lock-’em-up ideology” was the “animating force in legislatures, courtrooms, and district attorney’s offices across the country,” Colloff writes; the DA for Dailey’s case sought the death penalty for nearly every first-degree murder he came across. (This has changed somewhat over time, but a prosecutor’s job performance is still measured by conviction rate, and winning a high-profile case remains valuable political currency for DAs come election season.) For prosecutors, Skalnik was a gold mine. In recompense for his service, the state let him skirt the consequences of his latest misdeed: allowing him to walk free as he awaited his day in court despite a long history of skipping out on bail, offering him “extraordinarily lenient” plea deals, and even dismissing a charge of child molestation against him. Incredibly, this sort of exchange is an accepted aspect of the American justice system—Skalnik just fulfilled his end of the bargain with uncommon gusto and dedication. The men he sacrifices were little more than collateral damage.

Colloff has spent many years meticulously documenting structural problems with the criminal legal system through individual cases, working especially on wrongful convictions and the death penalty. She has surely had ample opportunity to appreciate just how challenging it is to get the public to care about capital punishment. The stories that can be found on death row are replete with suspense, remarkable details, and, well, life-and-death consequences. Yet any mention of the death penalty can provoke an instinctual recoil. Faced with such a repugnant facet of American life, most people find it easier to look away.

Advertisement

Colloff’s earliest long-form stories, for Texas Monthly, could be described as an elevated strain of true crime, and Catch the Devil likewise contains elements of the genre. Like many true crime narratives, the book is anchored by the murder of a young girl: on May 6, 1985, the naked, mutilated body of fourteen-year-old Shelly Boggio was found floating in the murky channel waters of Florida’s Gulf Coast. Dailey was incriminated by an acquaintance who told police that Dailey and Boggio drove away together on the night of the girl’s murder, but the state had no direct evidence against him—until Skalnik got involved. But Colloff deftly navigates past the major traps of the genre; though she doesn’t minimize the horror of Boggio’s death, she is less interested in the crime itself than in the other sorts of wrongdoing that abut and abet it.

There is the rampant, banal police and prosecutorial misconduct that accompanies wrongful convictions and that is hardly ever accounted for, even after an exoneration. There are the offenses that officials allow Skalnik to get away with, from petty financial fraud to serious felonies, in exchange for his testimony, “effectively giving him license to commit greater crimes,” as Colloff writes. (It’s impossible to know for sure, but there were likely even more made possible by Skalnik’s lies: when the system gets the wrong guy, it stops looking for the right one.) There is the moral sin—not in itself a crime, and almost never punished, even by professional censure—of keeping an innocent man in prison. (And Colloff leaves little doubt that Dailey is, indeed, innocent.) At his sentencing hearing, Dailey expresses his disillusionment with the American justice system. “At least in other countries you know ahead of time to expect that state witnesses will be brought against you, and that lies will be told,” he tells the court. “At least they don’t hide behind the facade of ‘truth and justice for all.’” And there is the relentless gendered violence that creates the conditions for such a senseless killing to occur. But only a murder will land you on death row.

Or it might, anyway. Most convicted murderers are not condemned to death. Boggio’s true assailant, who eventually confessed to the crime and lead detectives to the murder weapon, was sentenced to life in prison; he first came up for parole in 2010, twenty-four years after he was convicted. Dailey, a Vietnam veteran with severe PTSD who maintained his innocence throughout, had less luck with his jury.

It is precisely this sort of capriciousness that led the Supreme Court to abolish capital punishment in 1972. But the ban didn’t last long: after five states, including Florida, tried to address the justices’ concerns by establishing more clearly defined criteria for capital crimes, the Court reversed itself just four years later. (This history is recounted in Maurice Chammah’s 2021 book Let the Lord Sort Them, about Texas’s death row.) In the following years, Florida became the buckle in the “death belt,” the string of southern states, stretching to Texas, responsible for more than 90 percent of the late twentieth century’s executions. Pinellas County, where Skalnik was most active, was particularly bloodthirsty. Today, fifty years after the death penalty’s reinstatement, Florida remains an outlier, even among the few states still actively carrying out executions: Ron DeSantis’s fiefdom is now killing people at a “record pace,” according to a recent story by Colloff.1 It’s impossible to predict who will be next: an ACLU attorney tells her that the governor may as well be choosing his victims by “throwing darts at a list of names.” “Every afternoon,” Dailey says to one of his lawyers, “I wonder if they are going to come and get me.”

Catch the Devil grew out of an earlier feature Colloff wrote for The New York Times Magazine. Perhaps because she has already written about Skalnik and Dailey, her treatment of the Boggio murder here focuses on the flaws and sloppiness of the law enforcement investigation; she liberally doles out details that exonerate Dailey and reveal the true identity of the murderer, rather than withhold them for the sake of the typical true crime whodunit’s thrills. The suspense migrates elsewhere: Will the damning evidence of misconduct, procedural error, and the actual perpetrator’s sole guilt be enough to overcome the criminal legal system’s presumption of finality? (In an inversion of the pretrial presumption of innocence, it is very, very hard to undo a verdict once it’s been handed down.) Will Dailey’s succession of lawyers and investigators be able to secure the evidence they need, persuade crucial witnesses to recant, and overcome the postconviction process’s strictures to make the case for his innocence?

Advertisement

Other genre conventions are flipped on their head, too. More traditional innocence tales implicitly valorize the justice system by placing “wrongful convictions” in a category apart from all its other failings—treating them as aberrations. When I used the phrase in conversation with a prisoner on death row in Louisiana, he responded: “Let me ask you this: What is a wrongful conviction?” He had been sentenced to death for the murder of a prison guard during an escape attempt, after prosecutors withheld a statement from another inmate implicating two other escapees in the guard’s killing. Though Supreme Court Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson argued that this omission constituted textbook prosecutorial misconduct, the Court refused to even review the case.

By focusing on Skalnik and bringing in some of his other casualties, like the baby-faced teenager whom he painted as a calculating killer, Colloff shows how the systemic reliance on incentivized witnesses also leads to extreme overcharging—more banal than convicting an innocent man but no less harmful, given how pervasive the practice is and how accepted it remains. Her subject’s eagerness to lie about his fellow prisoners resulted in such devastating consequences only because countless detectives and prosecutors let it. Was this active malice, willful blindness, laziness, or some mélange of the three? Skalnik wasn’t exactly subtle in his methods, and he didn’t fool everyone: one prosecutor warned in a memo that he was not to be trusted, calling him “a BIG con artist.”

For those familiar with the relative impunity of law enforcement, it may not come as much of a surprise that in the early 1970s Skalnik briefly served as a police officer in Austin, Texas. He conducted himself about how you’d expect, badly injuring one Chicano man by clubbing him with his service weapon. (This was a harbinger of things to come: his first real snitch gig involved testifying against civil rights activists who were being prosecuted for protesting the brutal police killing of a Mexican laborer.) “As would become a pattern,” Colloff writes, “Skalnik wasn’t punished”; a federal civil rights probe into the incident went nowhere. Eventually he was caught writing bad checks and resigned, avoiding criminal prosecution or the humiliation of a dismissal. The book never goes so far as to suggest that becoming a cop set Skalnik down his path of destruction—clearly his pathology is more deeply rooted than that—but like many police officers, he clearly believes he is above the law. Colloff chooses these biographical details carefully, letting the rhymes and ironies appear self-evident. If anything, she probably could have been a bit more obvious; other readers might miss the critique. (They may also get lost in the maze of Dailey’s postconviction proceedings, despite her painstaking attempts to straighten out their twists and turns.)

Skalnik’s personal story is bizarre and singular, yet it’s remarkable—and telling—just how many wrongful convictions and death penalty cases follow the same basic trajectory as Dailey’s and share many of its features. Sixty percent of US exonerations since 1989 involved some form of official wrongdoing, and around one in three experienced prosecutorial misconduct. Jailhouse witnesses are a leading cause of wrongful convictions in capital cases; in one such Louisiana case that I wrote about, the snitch initially contacted prosecutors asking for leniency with his own case and claiming that he had extracted confessions from multiple fellow inmates.2 Prosecutors brought him in to testify that the accused, a total stranger, had confessed to him, sobbing; the Louisiana Supreme Court decision upholding the conviction ultimately credited him as “the state’s most telling witness.”

With far fewer resources than the prosecution, Dailey’s defense team didn’t investigate the murder on its own or present an alternative theory of what might have happened that night. His trial was brief—three and a half days—and jurors deliberated for a mere two hours. In capital cases, there is an additional stage after conviction called mitigation, during which the defense team is meant to present witnesses and material that might sway the jury toward mercy, but Dailey’s lawyers barely touched it, failing to mention the psychic wounds he incurred over months spent transporting killed and injured comrades during his first combat tour in Vietnam. After his conviction, his case was hamstrung time and again by turnover and cuts at the publicly funded firms that help death row prisoners navigate their appeals.

Colloff clearly sees her role as documentary rather than didactic. But faced with such an exhaustive litany of failure and abuse, the reader can’t help but wonder what is to be done, and there aren’t many answers in the book. She mostly saves the customary last-chapter solutions for her media interviews and editorials, but even these are hardly polemical: in a recent Washington Post op-ed she ventured that a review of all cases involving jailhouse witnesses might be undertaken and proposed that testimony from such figures “should also warrant closer scrutiny.” Catch the Devil notes merely that at least a dozen states have recently regulated the use of jailhouse informants and that “more radical ideas,” like a full ban on the practice, have stalled. The book’s damning final pages may leave readers hungry for something significantly more radical than even that.

While the book gives due credit to the many hardworking attorneys and investigators who have fought to free Dailey over the decades, there is little sense of a broader movement to make the death penalty once again a thing of the past. To be fair, more often than not these are isolated last-minute battles, focused on individuals just weeks or even days from death. Sometimes, miraculously, a reprieve comes: last November, on the morning that Tremane Wood was scheduled to be executed for a murder to which his brother had confessed, the governor of Oklahoma spared his life. Most often, it doesn’t: James Broadnax was put to death in April despite a confession from his codefendant. “No matter what you think about me, Texas got it wrong,” he said in his final statement.

For readers who are already convinced of the ills of the death penalty, Catch the Devil does not contain a great deal of moral complexity. Between the incorrigible Skalnik and the honorable Dailey, whose main personal failing is succumbing to alcoholism in the throes of his PTSD, Boggio’s murderer emerges as arguably the most interesting character, even as he remains secondary; the glimpses we get reveal a stunted man, troubled by an inchoate awareness that he has, after killing a teenager for the most pathetic of reasons, destroyed another man’s life as well—yet unable to atone for it in the one way that would actually matter.

It does, however, provide a portrait of lonely, aimless lives and the wreckage and pathology caused by war, addiction, alcoholism, and male sexual insecurity and rage. In this, and in its attention to minute biographical detail, it is an inheritor of earlier “nonfiction novels” like Norman Mailer’s The Executioner’s Song.

Before he goes off to war, Dailey is kind and openhearted, a young man who loves West Side Story and sings good-bye to his girlfriend, Mary Kay, every night. After his time in Vietnam, he’s a mess: racked by what we now understand to be post-traumatic stress disorder, drinking himself into a stupor every night. Mary Kay, now his wife, reluctantly divorces him, and the air force strongarms him into taking an honorable discharge. A quote from his mother about how the US military changed him and his brother—“I sent two lovely young men to the Air Force and Marines, and they came back, and they were different boys”—recalls the famous line uttered by the mother of one of the soldiers who participated in the My Lai massacre: “I sent them a good boy and they made him a murderer.”

Gendered violence and misogyny are so steady and relentless throughout Catch the Devil that they almost fade into the background, like a pulse. Boggio, the murdered girl, is a total void, a “ghost in her own narrative.” Colloff observes dryly that the only positive detail about her in a news article about the killing—written by two women, incidentally—comes from a truant officer who called the fourteen-year-old and her twin sister “really attractive.” During the time the girls were in middle school, five of their teachers were fired for sexual misconduct, including three for producing child pornography. Skalnik himself is not simply a larger-than-life scoundrel but also a predator: Colloff documents three instances of him abusing adolescent girls. The DA’s quid pro quo agreement to abandon charges in one of these cases constitutes the book’s most sickening instance of prosecutorial rot. The girl was asked to undergo a polygraph test; Skalnik was not.

And yet Colloff makes you see—sort of—how he might still be seductive to lonely women with limited horizons, accustomed to cruel or neglectful men. “Skalnik held out the promise of a life that was bigger, brighter, grander, and he made it feel thrillingly within reach,” she writes. He continues to collect wives well into his seventies, though he is in bad health; his late-stage bulk is described as “Falstaffian.”

Colloff’s overview of Skalnik’s life, from childhood to his old age and death in a Texas nursing home, presents a mitigation case of sorts; it’s more robust than the one the underfunded capital defense attorneys manage to throw together for Dailey, but still leaves something to be desired. We learn that Skalnik had an exacting and violent father, that his house was dilapidated compared with the others on the street, that he told people he was adopted—his “first big lie.” At times Colloff almost takes pains to appear disgusted by him; Catch the Devil is most affecting when she makes it clear that she, too, has been taken in by his promises to reveal everything about his past. In a book that includes graphic scenes of murder, molestation, and execution, the passages in which she visits Skalnik toward the end of his life are still the most unsettling, in part because he clearly unsettles her. This man mowed through countless lives: girls he abused, women he hoodwinked and discarded, men he sent to maximum security or death row. But when he starts to cry, recounting how his latest girlfriend didn’t pick him up from jail as promised, I felt a queasy sort of pity for him.

Skalnik’s lonely end is set against the bonds that Dailey has managed to maintain despite decades on the inside. Some of Colloff’s most moving insights into his experience on death row come from his years of correspondence with a Dutch woman, Marieke, who is part of the strange and touching volunteer army of women in the UK and Western Europe who write to and sometimes form romantic relationships with American capital prisoners. Just twenty-two when she first writes to him in 1998, Marieke becomes one of Dailey’s closest confidants: he jokingly refers to himself as “old man,” updates her on the vicissitudes of his case, and never fails to ask after her partner. In September 2019, when she learns that her pen pal has been assigned an execution, she sends him a greeting card that says, simply, “FUCK.”

Meanwhile Dailey’s ex-wife, Mary Kay, ends up marrying Dick, an air force buddy of his, but the two visit him regularly in prison. (Much earlier, in the depths of his addiction, he appraises their new life together with his kids, whom Dick has adopted, and tells the couple, “I wish you would adopt me.”) Two images from Catch the Devil remain with me: Dick, dying of rheumatoid arthritis and reliant on a wheelchair and oxygen tank, forcing his failing body to make the two-and-a-half-hour trip north so that he can see Dailey a few final times. And, after the execution date is finally set, Dailey and Mary Kay on opposite sides of a prison visitation table, their fingertips pressed up against the glass partition between them. These moments are notes of grace in a brutal and relentless book, reminders that even amid the harshest confinement some forms of freedom persist.

entries.title: Nightmares of History
entries.summary: The Newer World completes Sebastian Barry’s trilogy of novels about Americans caught up in the violence of the nineteenth century.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
The teenage Thomas McNulty ran away from Ireland during the Famine of the 1840s and fetched up under a hedge in Missouri, where he met another young wanderer, John Cole of New England. They became friends and eventually lovers, “two wood-shavings of humanity in a rough world,” pretty boys who found their first jobs as saloon girls in a mining town. They put on dresses and perfume, filled their bodices with cotton to provide “the illusion of the gentler sex” in a place without many women, and for fifty cents a night danced with anyone who happened by, the tavern’s owner standing ready with a shotgun to guard against any kissing or fumbling.

Then they join the army. Horses and uniforms, bad food and little water, a buffalo hunt and a sickening massacre in Northern California, with the cavalry riding into a peaceful Yurok village, shooting and stabbing until “there didn’t seem to be anything alive, including ourselves.” After that they fight on the Great Plains, muster out, and enjoy a stint as minstrel singers up in Michigan, though later they reenlist for the Civil War. Along the way the two men adopt a Lakota girl whose family their regiment killed. They call her Winona, Winona Cole, and after the war she goes with them to the broken-down Tennessee farm of a Unionist comrade named Elijah Magan, which they have to defend against the defeated Confederates who surround them and who mount a murderous dawn attack. Every now and then Thomas puts on an old dress to do the housework. And there two more people are added to this ad hoc family: the newly freed twins Rosalee and Tennyson Bouguereau.

That’s a thumbnail sketch of the Irish writer Sebastian Barry’s Days Without End (2016), a tall tale cast in the pungent eloquence of Thomas McNulty’s first person, a picaresque novel as grim as Cormac McCarthy and as hopeful as Huckleberry Finn.1 Its sequel, A Thousand Moons (2020), hands the narration to the now teenage Winona; the story is confined to the few square miles around the farm but marked by rape and murder and the terror of a hostile world.2 This household needs to keep its rifles ready, and the novel gives us her own memories of that morning assault. Nevertheless it too ends in hope, adding one person to the household and sending another away. Winona finds a partner in Peg, another young Native American woman, and Tennyson leaves for Fisk University in Nashville, one of the South’s first historically Black colleges. He has a fine voice and a deep knowledge of what W.E.B. Du Bois would call the “sorrow songs,” and in The Newer World, the third novel in the series, he becomes, for a time, a member of the Fisk Jubilee Singers, the a cappella group that took those songs from the quarters of the enslaved to the concert halls of Europe.

Born in 1955, Barry got off to a fast start, and a slow one. He published the first of his twelve novels, Macker’s Garden (1982), before he was thirty, but though he then produced a string of poems and plays, his career didn’t gain much traction until 1995, when The Steward of Christendom opened at the Royal Court Theatre in London. Imagine Beckett as a realist. It is 1932, and an old man named Thomas Dunne lies dying in an Irish county home, a broken-down ward of the state with his mind on the border between dementia and insanity. Once he was a powerful figure, a police superintendent who defended British rule and Dublin Castle against the ever-growing force of Irish nationalism, defended it even during the Easter Rising, though he is a Catholic. Now he flits between past and present. He talks to his daughter Annie and dreams of his son, who died in the Great War, he tries to justify what the new Ireland views as his treachery, and all the while he is badgered by the home’s attendant, Smith, who finds him as “mad as a barking stone mason” and tells him he shouldn’t talk to people who aren’t there.

The Steward of Christendom drew on the life of one of Barry’s great-grandfathers,3 and three novels about Thomas Dunne’s children followed—Annie Dunne (2002), A Long Long Way (2005), On Canaan’s Side (2011)—books whose main characters have a few common memories but wildly divergent lives: Annie, who can barely keep a place in this now independent land; the dead soldier boy, Willie; and Lily, who exchanges mad Ireland for Chicago. Along with the three more recent novels set in nineteenth-century America, there is a third set of three as well, one that begins with The Whereabouts of Eneas McNulty (1998), Barry’s first mature novel. It too draws on bits of his family history, and though it was written almost twenty years before Days Without End it contains an apparently throwaway reference to a long-ago relative who went to America and joined the army. Did Barry already have those later books in mind, a fictional world that existed before a word of it found paper? Or did he simply capitalize on that earlier hint?

Advertisement

Eneas McNulty is flung out into the world, and even less happily so than the cavalryman Thomas, hounded down the years by the IRA because of the choices he made when young. Its companion pieces in the McNulty series offer a pair of equally lonely lives. In The Temporary Gentleman (2014) Eneas’s brother Jack becomes an engineer and spends much of his life in Africa, a servant of the dying British Empire, while in The Secret Scripture (2008) his sister-in-law Roseanne commits a single indiscretion and is cast off by her husband, another Thomas McNulty, a rising man in the politics of the 1930s. She lives to be a hundred and spends more than sixty utterly lucid years in an insane asylum; put that alongside The Steward of Christendom and it’s enough to suggest that such confinement was once an inescapable part of Irish life. And Roseanne too remembers, though far more coherently than the old policeman, offering her own version of events in other novels. She thinks her way back to her early days in the country town of Sligo, on the island’s northwestern coast, and writes her story on whatever paper she can find, hiding her pages under a loose floorboard. Her father was a grave digger and then the city’s rat catcher; she worked as a waitress, liked to dance, and her blonde-haired beauty was a temptation to the town’s young men. Or so the local priest said, and he had her packed away as a nymphomaniac in the midcentury repression of Éamon de Valera’s Ireland.

Triptychs. That’s what Barry’s Irish trios are, three panels that make a whole but can nevertheless be detached and mounted separately. Each of the Dunne and McNulty books casts its light upon the others, and we learn more with every volume about these families’ distinctive histories. Yet within each group none of them can be said to come “first” in anything but their order of publication, and they can easily be read on their own. Two books in each group are in the first person, one is in the third, but there’s no sense of an ongoing narrative, a continuously developing story that binds these different characters together. In that sense these families are sundered; their lives touch and affect one another, but they are in no real sense shared.

The American books are very different. Days Without End can be read by itself, but I’m not so sure about the others—no, I’m sure that they shouldn’t be read that way. The narration may move from character to character, but they’re a trilogy, not a triptych; their telling is essentially linear. The later books don’t just allude to their predecessors, they rely on them, on what we already know of this world, and in reading we go steadily forward in time, with each volume adding a decade or so to the tale.

Still, Tennyson and Rosalee Bouguereau had a life before they entered this new kind of family, before Elijah Magan and his friends came back from the Civil War—Elijah or Lige, the son of the man who had once owned and then freed them. The Newer World begins with genealogy, Tennyson’s statement of who his people are: “My father Chas Bouguereau upped sticks some sixty years ago and left Louisiana”; he was a sugar planter’s son and a free man of color who if he’d had any sense would have gone on to Ohio instead of stopping in Tennessee, where “a free skin was an awkward suit.” A blacksmith with “a long shining face” who maybe could have passed, this clever, handsome, ever-laughing charmer fell for a girl on one of the plantations where he worked, got her pregnant, and tried to buy her freedom. But the price was high, $1,000 that he thought to get by robbing a bank a hundred miles away, and by the time Tennyson and Rosalee were born their father was dead, hanged “off a black-nut tree.” After that the girl’s enslaver—and probably also her father—found it embarrassing to keep her: It “wore away at his self-respect, though he likely had a lot to spare.” But he raised his price, selling her and her unborn children for $1,200 to old Luther Magan, which turned out to be their “main stroke of luck.”

Advertisement

None of that past figures in Days Without End or A Thousand Moons, in which we know Tennyson as a crack shot and a great singer but not as the dry ironist the lines I’ve quoted suggest. And I could go on quoting: at one point the Magan dogs are so thin with hunger that “they rattled when they ran.” Tennyson’s language is clipped, precise, and vivid, a language that’s not quite like that of Barry’s other narrators. Thomas comes to us in long loping loquacious sentences and reports what people say rather than reproducing it, with their speech embedded in his own; there’s not a single set of quotation marks in the entirety of Days Without End. Winona’s voice in A Thousand Moons feels as young as she is and reminds me a bit of Mattie Ross’s in Charles Portis’s True Grit (1968). She’s been educated by a country lawyer, has a good head for figures, and her written grammar is entirely correct, but when she speaks she might say, “I sorry…I always causing you trouble.” Tennyson is terse by comparison, and more drawn to sentence fragments, pointillist details that make a scene.

Early in The Newer World a Confederate troop rides up to the Magan place as the Civil War begins and requisitions Luther’s horses and mules. Tennyson watches, notes

that bright lamp of confidence in the faces. Beginning of the war. Could have lit their way with their faces in the dark. Oh, good as lamps…. Two hundred nostrils flaring and firing out steam, every horse stepping forward, stepping back.

They take the animals, then one of them spots Rosalee and asks “if ‘that girl yonder’ had been bred.” They drag her into an outbuilding, and all Tennyson can do is freeze, for “I had two hundred and forty years’ training in me not to move. No one can measure the shame of it.” But any movement would mean death, and he can help her more if he lives.

The man who rapes Rosalee is named Tim Petrie, and it’s the Petrie clan that after the war mounts the attack on the Magan farmhouse, with Tennyson using his prized Spencer carbine to drop one of the marauders, a “sudden red rose” on the man’s head at a distance of a hundred yards. No one outside that house will ever learn who made the shot, learn that he has killed a white man, but in The Newer World there’s something more to this scene. For when I first read Days Without End I could not have known, because Thomas did not know, the particular sense of justice and vengeance with which Tennyson pulled the trigger. The one version complements the other. It adds an extra layer of meaning, but nothing in these three books works, Rashomon-like, to contradict the others’ telling.

Different voices, characters, histories, each with its own part and experience in what nevertheless remains in every sense a shared story. For it’s not only the books that rely on one another—these characters do as well, in contrast to those in Barry’s Irish novels. They trust and need and never truly fail one another, their lives spent in something like communion.

There’s something else these books share. I said that I could go on quoting, by which I mean that reading Barry makes me want to quote: his every work is marked by a startling and at times exhilarating gift of phrase. That’s what binds his three very different trios together; that’s where his voice can be found. Sometimes it’s just a word: the skin as a suit, a single syllable turned metaphor, or the dogs rattling along. A simile, an image to remember, and usually a homely one, the language never purple, never even rich. As far back as Annie Dunne the lumps of turf in a hearth burn “slow as snails all night,” and when he first enters the army Thomas McNulty knows that “whisky would be our pillow.” In The Newer World a man caught in the siege of Vicksburg remembers that “we chewed our tongues for food.” These characters know pain; the pages that describe them are a sensuous delight.

The tongue chewer is called George, though his legal name is Pompey Jorgensen. When Vicksburg falls he joins a regiment of the United States Colored Troops, and afterward makes his way to Fisk. He’s the first student Tennyson meets there when after eighty pages The Newer World moves from the Magan farm to Nashville, a man who starts their friendship by cutting the newcomer’s hair and handing him a suit of clothes, everything down to his first set of underwear and a “black string tie.” Fisk is hard for Tennyson at first. He had learned to read and write as a child, attending an illegal school run by the local lawyer who later arranges his tuition and teaches Winona as well. But the classical curriculum is difficult, and he’s afraid when he’s asked to sing, believing that he doesn’t really know any songs, just the tunes that come from the field. “I thought I sounded like a toad that a water moccasin has bit,” he says, then he settles into the song and feels free. There will be much to learn, but his place is secure, and he soon finds another place, in the heart of a honey-voiced girl named Minnie, whose own memories are of Louisiana cane fields. The college’s strict rules work against any romance, and so they meet above all in the music. The songs they sing together evoke all the troubles they’ve seen, and yet the sounds they make from it are a balm that feels like “some kind of apology from God.”

Actually, Tennyson finds a place in two hearts. For there is also George, though Barry is coy about the precise nature of their relationship, one for which Tennyson seems to have few words. The historic Fisk Jubilee Singers raised money for the university by performing across Europe, including an 1873 appearance before Queen Victoria, and that’s where Barry sends his characters as well. Then during a concert “for miners and their ladies…George’s voice cracked like a branch” and pitched him into silence. They’re gone, his “beautiful notes,” and back in Nashville he decides to rejoin the army and become one of what were called the Buffalo Soldiers, the Black cavalry troopers who rode along the western frontier. That presents Tennyson with a choice, and The Newer World with a complicated formal challenge.

“History is a nightmare from which I am trying to awake.” Stephen Dedalus’s words in Ulysses are overfamiliar by now, but they’re still worth remembering, if only for the sake of contrast. No figure in the later history of Irish literature has had that particular bravado, and you might even say they know better. The nightmares in which Barry’s characters live have very particular shapes and names. There’s the Famine, and the English; there’s poverty, the ever-stifling Catholic Church, and the varied murderous forms of Irish nationalism. That history is explicit and visible, an explanatory force that is everywhere felt and recognized. It’s not the hidden hand that until recently has allowed so many white Americans, and white American writers, to think of themselves as exceptional and exempt. What reading Barry has made me see anew, however, is just how much of that history has happened abroad. The diaspora has been one of Irish fiction’s great subjects. England of course, for Protestants especially, the tradition that runs from Swift to Wilde and on to William Trevor. And America: there’s Brooklyn (2009), by Barry’s contemporary Colm Tóibín, but the line goes back at least as far as George Moore’s The Untilled Field (1903), in which country churches survive on remittances from the New World.

Thomas McNulty knows why he has come to America. He doesn’t entirely understand the Famine, but he knows that it left Ireland to starve “in her stocking feet. And she had no stockings.” It killed his mother and his sister; it made them all “only rats of people.” After that the army was a good life, and though in its ranks you might “meet a dozen men a month came from Ireland…you never hear them talk about it much.” Thomas recognizes that he is only a speck, something for the world to swat around; nevertheless he wants to survive, and does. Yet America to him is a kind of confusion. He’s clear about Ireland, he feels it in his bones, but why he’s sent to California or winds up for a time in Andersonville—all that’s a mystery. What he understands instead is loyalty: “I seen killer Irishmen and gentle souls but they’re both the same,” and he won’t hesitate to shoot a friend to save someone he loves.

The history that drives The Newer World is a different one, and I can imagine a reader who might question Barry’s decision to write from within it, or indeed in Winona’s voice in A Thousand Moons. He did, however, begin as a playwright, and a good playwright knows how to make characters of very different identities speak, how to give them a cadence and linguistic register of their own. The stage taught him “the efficacy of the first person,” he said in an interview, and added that as a writer “I am most fully interested in something I know almost nothing about,” in others and otherness, a sound, a phrase, a “hint of music” that he pursues until he finds where it comes from. A lot of reading lies behind The Newer World, and I suspect that there’s also a lot behind Days Without End. How else can we know the past? Still, Barry’s attempt to enter this world is also shaped and determined by Ireland. He’s written about the American West as far back as a play called White Woman Street (1992), which Fintan O’Toole describes as depending “on the irony of Irish natives, dispossessed on this side of the Atlantic, slaughtering and dispossessing Native Americans on the other side.” An irony indeed, but dispossession and loss are things that Barry’s own world knows about as well, and that give him a grasp on the inner life of those too often regarded, in O’Toole’s words, as the “footnotes…oddities…[and] quirks of history.”

He has had a long, complex, and much-laureled career. Both The Secret Scripture and Days Without End won the Costa Book of the Year award, making him the only novelist to receive it twice, and he’s often figured on the long or short lists for the Booker Prize, most recently for Old God’s Time (2023), the story of a retired and ever-haunted policeman, long-listed for the Booker and the winner of one of France’s major literary awards. The Newer World is not among his best books. Still, its problems are interesting, and seem to grow from a conflict between what might work in a freestanding novel and what this trilogy requires in the way of symmetry and resolution. The book thins out once the Jubilee Singers get to England. Tennyson is startled by the courtesy everyone shows them, and especially by the ducal palace in which they’re invited to stay, by “the absolute curious clockwork” with which it seems to run, “the eggs for breakfast, and the shoes taken away for polishing.” In what he calls a “sitting room” the paintings are “as high as a house,” and they settle themselves in deep chairs, “held captive by the cushions.” The phrasing keeps some of its brilliance, though the Dickensian notes with which he depicts that “clockwork” mansion don’t quite sound like him. And the irony with which he described his life in Tennessee here becomes a kind of wide-eyed naiveté.

Perhaps that’s inevitable, and in any case the book’s English chapters are nothing more than a bridge. The history of the Jubilee Singers may require them, but they’re really just the place for George’s voice to crack, leading Tennyson to decide to join the army with him. On the page that decision seems undermotivated—his voice is still good, and why choose his friendship with George over his love for Minnie? The sexual bond with her is clear, and eventually consummated. With George it goes largely unsaid, more unsaid than it needs to for someone who has lived with Thomas and John. I don’t like to second-guess a novelist’s decisions, but I can’t stop envisioning a different future for Tennyson, a forking path in which he stays at Fisk, marries Minnie, and eventually moves, as she does, into Nashville’s small Black middle class. Everyday urban life in a difficult nineteenth-century world, church and a job and children: that would be a rich subject in itself, and in many ways its depiction would be harder than that of the now-familiar army. It may even be one that Barry wants us to imagine, as if daring us to do that second-guessing. That’s bold, but it still leaves me wondering what exactly requires Tennyson to travel the same plains that his white friends once did.

The scenes out West are dramatic enough. As they ride the dust of the desert is “laid on us like a second uniform,” glued fast by sweat, and Tennyson has the political awareness to know that their job is “to cancel freedom,” to keep his Native American countrymen from living as they want. One night they camp under the rim of a canyon, only to be woken by a gunshot as an Apache band tries to stampede their horses. In the morning he finds George dead, his throat cut, maybe by a hatchet or “more likely one of the picket pins murderously flying about,” the sharp-edged pins with which they stake their horses at night. He feels that his whole life has gone into the ground with his friend and at first wants revenge, yet when his troop is poised and ready outside an Apache settlement he cannot help but think of Winona, and then of the attack on Lige Magan’s farm. Only a sudden hailstorm keeps them from riding in and saves him from becoming his own enemy. Worse will follow, and as his enlistment ends he will be a witness to the massacre at Wounded Knee.

That seems heavy-handed, at once powerful and obvious. It is also essential for the conclusion Barry wants to reach, the one that means he could not simply send Tennyson off into domesticity, however intriguing that prospect might be. As part of a trilogy The Newer World needs something different than it might on its own. It needs its narrator to be utterly broken, drained, alone, and walking back toward home, unsure of what he will find there, or even if anyone on the Magan place is still alive. Because now an opportunity presents itself, a consequential choice of a kind he could not have made in Nashville. Both of the earlier books end with a death averted, with the trial and possible execution of one of its main characters. It’s different in The Newer World, and yet not. For here Tennyson stands as the would-be executioner. He spots an old enemy riding along a country road, confident and carefree; he steps into the woods, well hidden, and takes out the repeating rifle that has been his companion for years, “five bullets sitting in the butt.” He draws a bead, waits, and then, hardly knowing why, he throws the weapon away.

Whatever the bobbles of this novel’s second half, that is the necessary ending to the sequence of violent books to which it belongs. He puts down the gun and steps off into his uncertain future. That may say something about America, and about what has never really happened here. I’m pretty sure that for Sebastian Barry it also says something about Ireland.

entries.title: Interview with a Bandit
entries.summary: Many Nigerians have turned to violence after years of suffering under widespread government corruption.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
Were it not for his AK-47, you wouldn’t think Babangida—a lanky, dark-skinned, soft-spoken man in his late thirties, wearing a traditional caftan and a colorful cloth cap—was the type to harm anyone. Yet he is one of some 30,000 gunmen, known locally as “bandits,” who for the past fifteen years have terrorized a huge swath of Nigeria’s countryside, from the dusty villages of the state of Sokoto in the northwest to the lush farmlands of the state of Benue in the central region. Without warning, gangs of them—some with just a dozen or so members, others with hundreds—swoop into towns and villages on motorcycles, loot and destroy property, and kill or kidnap people for ransom. Thousands have lost their lives in the mayhem, and hundreds of thousands have fled their homes to escape it.

After months of negotiation, Babangida agreed to an interview with one of us, the Agence France-Presse journalist Aminu Abubakar, in a remote village in his home state of Katsina, in the country’s northwest. The village lies down an unpaved track, far from the highway. Its few hundred inhabitants live in mud huts with grass-thatched roofs, amid baobab, acacia, and neem trees. In the surrounding fields they grow corn, sorghum, and other crops and keep goats, chickens, and cows. They get around mostly by bike, motorcycle, and oxcart. No one owns a car.

Last December, in what President Donald Trump called a “Christmas present,” Washington launched air strikes on Sokoto, claiming to combat what US lawmakers and evangelical groups have called a genocide against Christians committed by bandits, most of whom are Muslim, and by other armed groups, including the Islamic State. The US, alleging violations of religious freedom, put Nigeria on a watch list of Countries of Particular Concern. The Christian genocide claim is highly dubious: most of the bandits’ victims have been Muslims, not Christians, and only about 5 percent of violence against civilians has targeted Christians for their faith, according to Armed Conflict Location and Event Data, a respected monitoring group. But when experts try to explain what is actually going on, they tend to cite a vague array of social, economic, and political factors, including historical grievances, climate change, weak governance, and resource scarcity, none of which points to straightforward policy solutions.

Upon hearing US lawmakers characterize the bandits as Islamist fanatics, a Nigerian government conflict mediator who had befriended Babangida urged him to tell his side of the story to the world, which is how he came to speak with Aminu. Throughout the interview, he gripped his AK-47, its barrel pointed to the sky. He had been a bandit for nearly a decade but said he didn’t know how many raids he’d participated in or how many people he’d kidnapped or killed. “We don’t keep records,” he said. But “no bandit just picked up a gun overnight and turned to violence. There is always a story behind it. Let me tell you mine.”

Born in 1988 into a family of Fulani pastoralists, Babangida grew up in a village even more remote than the one where Aminu met him. It had no school, no clinic, no running water, no electricity, and virtually no other modern amenity. His family was not rich; they had about a hundred cows, whereas some had thousands. But they managed to eke out a living by subsistence farming and selling milk.

As a child, Babangida and the other village boys would typically rise early and take their families’ animals out to the fields for grazing, then return in the late afternoon. They would bring along some millet gruel and water, a stick for prodding the cattle, a machete for cutting tall grass, and a transistor radio to listen to music and the news. His most vivid childhood memory is of his circumcision at age seven. Neighbors and relatives gave the boy a flock of chickens. His family feasted on some of them right away and sold the rest to buy a goat, which Babangida raised. He married at eighteen, and after his first child was born the following year, his family gave him a bull and two heifers, which he bred while continuing to help out with his family’s herds.

Every year, with the approach of the dry season, Babangida’s family and thousands of others headed south with their animals in search of pasture and returned in time for planting. This custom—known as the transhumance—has been shaped by centuries of adaptation to one of the world’s harshest environments. It usually lasts for months and may cover hundreds of miles. The herders are seeking water during the dry season and escaping the Harmattan winds, which blow down from the Sahara, causing dust storms that reduce visibility to a few meters and sometimes send haze across the ocean to Florida.* The herder migration routes avoid the breeding grounds of the sleeping sickness–carrying tsetse fly, which swarms from the Sahara’s edge to the southern forests with the rains, and they follow the growth of fodder that produces the best milk. Acacia tree leaves, for example, which goats love, are 20 percent protein, and baobab leaves have fifteen times as much calcium per gram as milk does.

Advertisement

This was the only life Babangida knew. He expected that one day he’d have his own herd and become independent. But ecological and social forces that had been gathering for at least a decade before he was born soon shattered this modest dream.

In the past, herders tended to arrive in the southern farming regions in time for the cows to eat the stubble in the fields and fertilize them for the next planting season—an arrangement that worked for everyone. But since the droughts of the 1970s the transhumance has been pushed farther south. Meanwhile the sedentary population has grown and farms have spread into areas designated by the government in the 1960s as grazing reserves. Local officials, including village chiefs, police, and even the military, have done little to stop farmers from encroaching into grazing areas, and some have colluded with them. Now herders might pass through a grazing area on their way south only to find it under cultivation on the way back, Babangida said. They have no choice but to herd their animals through the new crop rows, causing quarrels with angry farmers that over the years have become increasingly protracted and violent.

Farmer–herder conflicts are not new in this part of the world, but they were rarer in the past and were usually resolved by elders from both sides who constituted an informal justice system largely invisible to Nigeria’s colonial occupiers and coup-prone postindependence governments. Fulani elders, known as ardos, would accompany the transhumance and form relationships of mutual aid with other ardos and farmer elders along the way, negotiating fair compensation for lost animals or crops. But these days Fulani elders are far less likely to accompany the transhumance, preferring to engage in sedentary—and safer—activities like farming or preaching the Quran. Commercialization has also weakened the delicate diplomacy that sustained the transhumance for thousands of years. Today young herders increasingly work for investors, government officials, or wealthy agriculturalists rather than their own families. When conflicts over trampled crops arise, these herders are more likely to try to pay off the farmers rather than rely on long-standing relationships among elders to negotiate and maintain harmony, says the West Africa expert Matthew Turner.

As traditional justice mechanisms eroded, the government failed to fill the vacuum, and sometimes made things worse. Nigeria’s police are notoriously corrupt and often biased against herders, a subject Babangida was eager to discuss. “Say a herder destroys a piece of a farmer’s field,” he explained.

The village chief will set the fine well beyond the value of the crops destroyed. But when a farmer kills a herder’s cattle, it’s declared the herder’s fault and he receives no compensation. If the chief calls the police, they will connive with a judge to raise the fine even more, so the herder is wiped out. If the farmer was injured or killed, all hell breaks loose and the chief, police, and judge make fortunes out of us.

One reason for this perceived anti-Fulani bias is that it is usually farmers from the communities where the police are stationed who initiate complaints about their trampled fields. Fulani pastoralists have also long been looked down upon as backward and uncivilized by the sedentary people of northern Nigeria, most of whom belong to the Hausa ethnic group. The supposedly hapless Fulani are the butt of endless Hausa jokes, and you can sense their injured pride in their terse and taciturn demeanors.

Another problem is that the police, woefully under-resourced like virtually all public services in Nigeria, frequently collude with brutal vigilante squads made up of volunteers from local farming communities. These militias, formed as a response to banditry by Fulani herders, have been portrayed in the media as informal peacekeepers, but to the Fulani they are a terrifying scourge responsible for wanton attacks on farmsteads, cattle rustling, and even murder. It was a series of such attacks that changed Babangida’s life and that of his community forever.

“One night,” Babangida said, “our village was invaded by vigilantes, [who were] assisted by police. They broke into our home, arrested my mother and younger brother, and took ninety-seven cattle”—nearly all they owned. Babangida had no idea why his family was targeted. It may have been retribution for alleged offenses carried out by other Fulani or just theft.
