For the Fulani, cows are not mere material possessions. Each one has a name, and wherever they wander, the lead cow always knows her way home. Stolen cows will sometimes grunt and pull at their ropes when their true owners come searching for them in a crowded market—even before their owners recognize them. Some thieves have even been caught this way.

Babangida’s family was not so lucky:

We finally found the cows in Gusau [a city in the neighboring state of Zamfara]. The police demanded 1.8 million naira [about $1,300] to bail my mother and brother out. Eventually we managed to get ten of our cows back too, but I sold them to buy guns, one of which I’m holding now.

He didn’t know where it came from: “If you have money, suppliers will bring guns to your doorstep.”

Babangida and his family moved to a bandit community in the forest. “Our cattle were gone,” he said; his life as a herder was over. He knows of many other Fulani who were pushed into banditry this way:

The same policeman who took our herd stole 480 cows and 300 goats from another herder. After lengthy court proceedings, he was given a few animals back, but the case has been transferred to a higher court and there is no information about the animals he lost.

The parents of a young woman he knows set out on a trip to inform relatives about her upcoming wedding. Their bus was flagged down at a vigilante checkpoint. Because they were Fulani, they were singled out, pinned to the ground, and slaughtered. “A vigilante doesn’t verify who is a criminal and who is not,” Babangida said. “If you are Fulani, he just slits your throat when he gets you.”

“The son of that couple who were killed had a baby,” he went on.

He took five cows to the market to raise money for the naming ceremony, but when he arrived, he was arrested on suspicion that they’d been stolen. He was never a thief, and those cows were his, but his family had to sell more cows to get him released, and the original five were never returned. The naming ceremony and his sister’s wedding were still pending, so he took another seven cows to another market, where he was arrested yet again and the cows seized. More cows were sold to get him released, but the original seven were never returned.

Some of this man’s friends were bandits, and they pressured him to join them. At first he resisted, but he eventually gave in and the share he got from looting, plus contributions from other bandits, enabled him to pay for the wedding and the naming ceremony. He is now a bandit commander.

Five years ago vigilantes claiming to be smoking out bandits stormed the settlement of another of Babangida’s kinsmen and left with six hundred cows. “Two of his brothers were killed, but he managed to hide in a disused water tunnel attached to a military outpost. His parents disappeared that day, never to be seen again. One day, while searching for them in a nearby village on a market day, he was introduced to Dogo Gide,” a notorious bandit with ties to Ansaru, an al-Qaeda affiliate. Dogo Gide trained him to use a gun and then sent him to a subsidiary camp, where he now leads a kidnapping-for-ransom team.

President Trump’s claims of a Christian genocide puzzled Babangida: “Most of our victims are Muslims of the Hausa ethnic group, not Christians.” He admitted that “some bandits say they are waging jihad or striving for the sake of Allah,” and others collaborate with groups like al-Qaeda for strategic reasons. But for most bandits, “it is all about making money and revenge.”

“Years of injustices are what pushed Fulani herders into banditry,” he went on.

We were never criminals before. Wherever you see indiscriminate killings and destruction it is usually a revenge attack against other killings. Yes, the people we attack and kidnap have nothing to do with what happened to us, but the ones who robbed us are doing the same thing.

Today older bandits are being replaced by a younger generation that relies for courage on drugs—marijuana, diazepam, tramadol, codeine, whatever is cheap and easy to obtain. Stoned young bandits can become so savage that they sometimes kill hostages even after ransom is paid. Babangida and the other older bandits are terrified of them.

In the past fifteen years Nigeria has spent some $44 billion battling armed groups, including bandits, with little to show for its efforts. The army has launched air strikes on militant hideouts, set up roadblocks, and tried to cut off bandit communications. This has resulted in many bandit deaths and arrests but no reduction in attacks. In February Washington sent some two hundred soldiers to assist the Nigerian military fighting armed groups in northern Nigeria. But the violence only increased, and they were withdrawn in September.

In 2019 the Nigerian federal government announced that it would spend some $300 million to create ranches that would provide herding settlements with grazing facilities. The funding and political leadership did not materialize, and the project was roiled with controversy because locals fear any development that would lead to permanent herder settlements near their villages and farms, and they also wanted to see justice and the return of displaced people, not ranches for those they perceive as their tormentors. The government revived the scheme in August, but because of rainfall variability, the ranches will have to be enormous for it to work.

Local government officials have also tried to negotiate with bandits, offering amnesty as well as improved schools and hospitals if they lay down their guns. But these deals usually collapse, Babangida said, because the government fails to deliver on its promises.

For example, under the terms of a peace agreement in the state of Katsina, a school for herder children was built but was then converted into a military barracks. A former governor also provided funds to help bandits find another trade, but his officials stole the money. The governor then announced that any bandit without a herd would be given a bull and a cow. The funds were disbursed, but not a single Fulani got anything. Eventually any repentant bandits returned to their guns.

Bandits and vigilantes are not the only ones responsible for violence in Nigeria. The country is also beset with armed robberies, kidnappings, extrajudicial and ritual killings, secessionist agitation, and attacks by so-called unknown gunmen, whom everyone knows but is afraid to name. On Nigeria’s university campuses, gangs with names like Black Axe and Second Sons of Satan stockpile weapons, fight rival gangs, initiate new members through rape, and burn the cars of professors who don’t give them good grades.

Like Babangida, many experts attribute this chaos to injustices resulting from government corruption that force people to feel they must take matters into their own hands. Corruption exists everywhere, but as the late historian of Africa Stephen Ellis argues in This Present Darkness: A History of Nigerian Organized Crime (2016), Nigeria has long seemed like a special case.

West Africans call it “stomach infrastructure” or “the politics of the belly,” and it takes countless forms, including the embezzlement and looting of Treasury funds, vote buying, electoral fraud, kickbacks from artificially inflated government contracts, ghost workers, petty bribery of police, judges, and other government officials, tribalism, and nepotism. Nigeria is Africa’s third-richest country, but because of corruption, many of its public clinics and schools barely function. This helps explain why in the northern region, where Babangida lives and where banditry is most common, nearly 20 percent of children die by age five and only a third of adults can read.

Why is corruption so entrenched in Nigeria and so many other African countries? It’s not as though no one’s aware of it. The continent’s militaries often launch coups on the pretext of fighting corruption; the struggle for democracy is justified in the same way. Both jihadist and fundamentalist Christian movements across Africa claim the same anticorruption mission. Even Babangida sees himself as fighting for law and order.

Like nearly every Nigerian head of state before him, President Bola Tinubu campaigned on an anticorruption platform. Once in office, he sacked some corrupt officials and hired as his national security adviser Nuhu Ribadu, who was honored by the World Bank for his heroic anticorruption work. Tinubu also unveiled a justice reform program designed to reduce official corruption and speed up the resolution of cases, although implementation may take decades, and so far ordinary Nigerians have seen little change.

But President Tinubu’s government has also given lucrative contracts to his business associates and his own family members, and he appointed as Nigeria’s minister of budget and economic planning Abubakar Atiku Bagudu, a former state governor linked to the predatory Nigerian dictator Sani Abacha, who stole billions from the Treasury in the 1990s. In 2025 Ribadu was reported to have secretly paid bandit groups and Boko Haram millions of dollars in ransom—in contravention of a 2022 Nigerian law against such payments, which have been shown to increase incentives for kidnapping—in order to secure the release of hundreds of hostages.

Perhaps Nigeria’s struggle with corruption, and the violence that appears to be linked to it, has something to do with the pace at which it has been forced to modernize. In an insightful 1999 essay, the anthropologist Jean-Pierre Olivier de Sardan suggested that colonialism imposed a weak Western-style bureaucratic system—which officially condemns corruption but does virtually nothing about it—on top of strong and long-standing social networks of mutual aid that all but obligate people in power to take advantage of enrichment opportunities and share their good fortune with kin. In other words, everyone hates corruption, but those in power would be shunned by their relatives as selfish if they didn’t engage in it.

Chinua Achebe saw it coming at independence. In his novel No Longer at Ease (1960), an idealistic, Western-educated government office worker in Lagos finds himself deep in debt as a result of the mounting demands of his family and the elders in his home village who paid for his European education. Despite his lofty moral convictions, he accepts a hefty bribe and is arrested. This helps explain how corruption can be so ubiquitous, though everyone—even bandits like Babangida—complains about it day and night. Ultimately, Babangida said, “justice is the only way out. When justice is upheld, everyone will live in peace.” No doubt many in Nigeria, including his victims and their avenging vigilantes, would agree.

entries.title: The Tightrope Walker
entries.summary: How did Trump manage to turn a failed coup d’état into a story of his own martyrdom?
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
Had you found yourself, these past pre-midterm months, obsessively appalled by the dark signs and wonders coming out of Washington: the stunningly unqualified people elevated to high office, the systemic corruption, self-dealing, and abuse of power, the undermining of the country’s alliances, the illegal tariffs, the catastrophic war of choice in the Middle East, and on and on? You had a right to be appalled, of course, but not to be surprised. This is the president, after all, who more than five years ago exhorted his followers to stage a violent coup on national television in which at least five people died. Afterward the federal government indicted and convicted nearly 1,300 rioters who had assaulted police, ransacked the Capitol, and tried to halt the peaceful transfer of power. Those felons had acted on the public encouragement of the outgoing forty-fifth president of the United States, and he pardoned them all on the first day of his second term. Which leads to a simple question: How is it that the only president in US history to mount a coup d’état was ushered back to the White House four years later by a plurality of American voters? As we gaze in queasy fascination at the clamorous combat playing out in Washington, what does it say about the world’s most powerful state that it was unable to defend itself against such a threat? Was it somnolence, or decadence, or a simple failure of imagination?

In the bright, cold early morning of January 6, I found myself wandering the otherworldly precincts of the Washington Monument, a few hundred yards from the Ellipse, where the president was soon to speak.* It took me a moment to realize that I had stumbled into an armed camp. Bearded men in tactical vests. Guys in MAGA hats checking sidearms on their hips. A man sighting in an assault rifle. And yet had I not told friends, when they asked why I was flying to Washington for January 6, that I was “going to attend Trump’s coup”? It was a joke, but only barely. “Big protest in D.C. on January 6th,” the president had tweeted on December 19. “Be there, will be wild!” The evidence of what was to come was splashed all over the Internet. But I could not yet quite grasp what I was seeing.

By its end tens of millions of people had witnessed the brutality of that day on national television, and it is brought back to savage life in Mary Clare Jalonick’s Storm at the Capitol: An Oral History of January 6th. “I can just remember my breath catching in my throat,” recalls the Capitol Police officer Caroline Edwards,

because what I saw was just a war scene…. There were officers on the ground. You know, they were bleeding. They were throwing up. I saw friends with blood all over their faces. I was slipping in people’s blood. I was catching people as they fell. It was carnage. It was chaos. I can’t even describe what I saw.

What looked like bloody medieval chaos—and, with all the bear spray and tear gas and blood and vomit, stank like it—was in fact a uniquely postmodern coup d’état: loosely organized online with various highly adaptable moving parts, inspired by the president of the United States. Tens of thousands of Trump foot soldiers came determined to “stop the steal.” Mixed in with these loyalists, many of them armed, were more organized groups of paramilitaries who were determined, as the Oath Keepers leader Stewart Rhodes put it on January 4, to support “President Trump’s fight to defeat the enemies foreign and domestic who are attempting a coup, through the massive vote fraud and related attacks on our Republic.” This “mirror language”—we must prevent a coup (in fact, attempt a coup)—is an increasingly unavoidable feature of our age that stems from the ongoing battle over legitimacy: Who exactly was mounting the coup? The paramilitaries saw themselves as following in the footsteps of the revolutionary forces of old to prevent a coup by the Washington establishment against their rightful president. By early afternoon, Jalonick notes, they “were headed toward the Capitol.”

The coup was free form, improvisatory, adaptive—that is, very Trumpian. Evidence suggests that after his speech Trump was vaguely planning to drive to the Capitol, mount the steps, confront his vice-president directly, and persuade him by force of will to accept the slates of fake electors that had been forged and signed in the seven swing states over the past weeks, or at least to send the votes back to the state legislatures. When, despite his angry insistence, Trump’s Secret Service agents refused to take him there, he sat alone before the television in the dining room off the Oval Office and, wielding his telephone and his tweets, guided his thousands of supporters. I clearly recall the moment when, deep in the huge motley wave trooping toward the Capitol, a woman near me festooned in American flag garb bent over her phone and shrieked, “Pence has thrown us under the bus!” Jalonick’s witnesses describe the moment:

Advertisement

Jessica Watkins, US Army veteran and bar owner, Oath Keepers, Ohio: So before we left the Ellipse, like, the crowd was real, real thick. And then, like, everybody—like, literally everybody—just started pulling out their phones. They were like, “Pence betrayed us. Pence betrayed us.” Like, we have to go….

Jason Dolan, former marine, Oath Keepers, Florida: I think you kind of felt a palpable feeling where the crowd went from being pretty—a pretty happy, joyful crowd to a pretty kind of pissed-off crowd.

This dark metamorphosis was entirely owed to Trump. It was 2:24 when the president, still watching the crowd on television and perhaps having finally conceded that his coaxing and threats had failed to persuade the vice-president to “do the right thing,” tweeted, “Mike Pence didn’t have the courage to do what should have been done,” and the crowd turned very ugly. The shouts of “Hang Mike Pence!” began, and Trump was quickly informed by a panicked White House aide of the vice-president’s peril. “So what?” the president responded. Even as the crowd surged wildly through the Capitol and the vice-president and then the senators and representatives hunkered down in fear for their lives, the president was personally lobbying senators to delay certifying the election:

Sen. Mike Lee, R-UT: Moments after the proceedings in the Senate were halted by the Capitol Police, my phone rang. The caller ID indicated that the call was coming from the White House…. To my great surprise, it was…President Trump on the other end of the line….

Sen. Tommy Tuberville, R-AL: When he brought me the phone, it said “White House” on it. It was the president.

Sen. Mike Rounds, R-SD: And so I was sitting here, and Coach [Tuberville] is right next to me. And the conversation…basically there’s a lobbying effort going on….

And he says, “Well, Mr. President, I gotta go. I guess they’re gonna get us out of here now.” And I never forgot that. Because while we were in the room, and there was enough going on to where they were going to remove us, there was still a lobbying effort going on by the president of the United States to stop the ballot from moving forward.

Amid the overwhelming violence at the Capitol, Trump was still single-mindedly determined to triumph over the system and remain in office.

What do you do with the perpetrator of a failed coup d’état who also happens to be president? What do you do with a chief of state who commits a crime against the state? The framers were familiar with such cases from their classical educations. They knew of Catiline, who in 63 BCE plotted to overthrow the Roman Republic and was killed battling republican troops. Had he survived, Cicero—serving as consul at the time—certainly would have had him executed. And of course they knew of Julius Caesar, whom a group of senators, in the belief that they were defending the republic, assassinated shortly after he’d named himself dictator. In both cases, a crime against the state was punished with the most severe sanction. In our own era, the little-known ex-corporal Adolf Hitler mounted the hapless Beer Hall Putsch in Munich against the Weimar Republic, served nine months in prison—he used them to dictate Mein Kampf, which became a best seller—and a decade later was named chancellor of Germany. In perhaps the closest parallel, Alberto Fujimori, who in 1992 mounted what in Peru was called an autogolpe (self-coup), was eventually imprisoned. (Peruvians recently elected his daughter president.) It is hard to think of a leader who mounted a failed coup going free only to be reelected four years later.

In this as in so many other things Donald Trump is singular. His decade at the pinnacle of our political life has been a stress test for our constitutional system and again and again has shown it to be badly wanting. If anything qualifies as the high crimes deserving of impeachment and conviction—with their accompanying banishment from high office—it was his actions on January 6. And yet the senators, having borne witness to his crimes, came ten votes short of convicting him.

Mitch McConnell, who as the Senate Republicans’ leader bears perhaps the greatest responsibility for that failure, put the matter squarely to his colleagues and the country:

There is no question—none—that President Trump is practically and morally responsible for provoking the events of the day. No question about it. The people who stormed this building believed they were acting on the wishes and instructions of their president.

He then concluded, “We have no power to convict and disqualify a former office holder who is now a private citizen.” (McConnell neglected to mention that he himself was responsible for delaying the Senate trial.) Not to worry, McConnell went on: “President Trump is still liable for everything he did while he was in office as an ordinary citizen…. He didn’t get away with anything yet. Yet. We have a criminal justice system in this country.”

Advertisement

Whether McConnell was sincere in his professed belief that the Constitution forbids the conviction of a private citizen or merely was seeking to avoid the political retribution a vote for conviction would have brought from the tens of millions of Republicans who still worshiped Trump, he had in effect, by blocking Trump’s conviction, handed the hot potato off to someone else. For that criminal justice system he praised so highly was now in the hands of President Joseph R. Biden.

Or rather in those of Biden’s attorney general, Merrick B. Garland. The incoming Democratic administration, and Garland in particular, had pledged to “depoliticize” a Justice Department that was thought to have been badly corrupted. Trump had publicly excoriated his first attorney general, Jeff Sessions, for failing to “protect” him, had summarily fired the FBI director, James Comey, for investigating what Trump called “the Russia hoax,” and had ordered that the special prosecutor named to carry out that investigation, Robert Mueller, be fired, too. These were all shocking departures from how business had been done in the Justice Department since its reconstruction after the abuses of the Nixon administration. For decades, write Carol Leonnig and Aaron C. Davis in their meticulous account, Injustice: How Politics and Fear Vanquished America’s Justice Department, veterans of the department warned young prosecutors

of Justice’s past failures to be transparent and impartial. Such violations risk undermining public confidence in the justice system….

Through the passage of decades, Justice has become a living, breathing organism of dedicated public servants yoked together to uphold these shared values in Republican and Democratic administrations. They pledged to keep Justice blind and impartial—and independent from political influence. They agreed that the facts and the law would guide their decisions on whether to charge a suspect or drop a prosecution when the evidence warranted.

Admirable words but perhaps a touch high-minded: one needn’t go back to Nixon to find persuasive instances of the Justice Department acting politically.

Still, there is no question that Garland, who had been a distinguished prosecutor and then a respected federal judge—and whom McConnell and his Republican majority refused a hearing in 2016 after Barack Obama nominated him to the Supreme Court—believed strongly in these principles. “As everyone who watched yesterday’s events in Washington now understands,” Garland said, after the president-elect introduced him on January 7, “the rule of law is not just some lawyer’s turn of phrase, it is the very foundation of our democracy.” And coming into office after Trump, how could he not be painfully aware, as Leonnig and Davis remind us, that the “department’s political independence…was never protected under law, but instead flourished through American presidents’ shared respect for this core precept”? It was these weak points in the governing structure—longtime practice dictated by norms, not laws—that Trump had been quick to sniff out and exploit. In doing so, he had left the Justice Department and the FBI skittish and politically traumatized.

By the time Garland was confirmed as attorney general in early March 2021, the Department of Justice was already fully engaged in a vast effort to prosecute the thousands who had breached the Capitol on January 6. Using cell phone data and videos posted to the Internet, hundreds of FBI agents and prosecutors identified and built cases against those who had bloodied police officers, smashed the Capitol doors and windows, and invaded the Senate and House chambers. As Garland had explained during his confirmation hearings, “We begin with the people on the ground, and we work our way up to those who are involved, and further involved, and we will pursue these leads wherever they take us.” There would be, that is, no leapfrogging to more powerful figures who actually might have planned and directed what happened that day or incited it with their ringing words to the crowd.

Garland was right that for many crimes this is standard law enforcement procedure: drug trafficking, for example. But to move against the suspected planners and directors of the coup—notably, the former president of the United States—would expose Garland’s beloved DOJ to charges that it was acting in the cause of political retribution. And did not the new attorney general, as he had said at his confirmation hearings, want “to turn down the volume on the way in which people view the department—that the Justice Department not be the center of partisan disagreement”? Investigating the former president for fomenting a coup was not exactly the way to regain the DOJ’s reputation for bipartisanship, even if the crime had been witnessed by the entire country. And it was not simply Garland’s determination to “right the ship at Justice.” The new attorney general “had told a few friends,” according to Leonnig and Davis, that he hoped that the country on January 6 “had in fact ‘burst a bubble’ of hyperpartisanship” and that in its aftermath the United States “was ready to pick up the pieces and move on, as it had after Watergate.”

For a nonpartisan attorney general this would seem a remarkably political basis on which to decline to investigate directly the author of the greatest political crime in the country’s history. Not only did the judgment prove to be strikingly ill founded, it blithely assumed that the threat to the state had passed. Whatever the reason, because of his reluctance to have the DOJ seen to be acting “politically,” Garland and his top associates proved willing essentially to put aside clear evidence that Trump, Roger Stone, Rudolph Giuliani, and others had committed crimes in trying to nullify the results of a national election—evidence that became impossible to deny once the House’s January 6th Committee began holding its hearings. And Garland was not alone. Leonnig and Davis describe how FBI investigators also proved “a little gun-shy of tangoing with Trump again.” Trump’s relentless, savage criticism of the FBI and the DOJ had had its effect. From the White House he had indefatigably worked the refs by denouncing them over “the Russia hoax,” among other things, and the refs were now unwilling to risk further provoking him.

As for higher-level officials at the FBI, many “saw the Capitol attack investigation as a political minefield if they leapt to pursue a former president or his aides at this stage.” Obviously they were right. But does it follow that both the crime against the state and its perpetrators should go uninvestigated? Going forward with an investigation, of course, was certain to sharpen the department’s own political divisions. Injustice is perhaps at its best in showing these internal political stresses as the various January 6 cases progressed. FBI agents in red states slow-walked or refused to interview witnesses or even execute arrest warrants. “On multiple occasions,” Leonnig and Davis write, “prosecutors had groused that agents had even resisted investigative steps involving members of the Proud Boys, who had helped lead the charge, breaking windows and forcing their way into the Capitol.” Elsewhere agents questioned why “grandmothers and blue-collar dads who seemed to have followed the mob” would be charged with any crime more serious than trespassing. Meanwhile Garland’s reluctance to investigate those who had led the coup was attracting critics within the department who

worried an obsession with safeguarding the perception of an apolitical DOJ was interfering with its core mission in a moment with little historical precedent. To them, the department couldn’t uphold the rule of law without bringing the most senior people responsible for January 6 to justice.

After the failed coup, was anyone who could make decisions within the federal government concerned to protect the country from its perpetrator? Acquitted in the Senate, Trump had regained his grip on the Republican Party and begun leading a campaign of retribution against members who had voted for his impeachment. Party leaders flocked to Mar-a-Lago to kiss the ring. The former president was growing more powerful by the day, with the same unmatched ability to command the news cycle at his pleasure or his whim.

Would the United States government ever have indicted the president who staged a coup against it had the House’s January 6th Committee not blazoned, in the summer of 2022, the damning evidence of his crimes all over prime-time television? Garland finally let himself be forced to select a special counsel to investigate “whether any person or entity unlawfully interfered with the transfer of power following the 2020 presidential election” only on November 18, 2022, nearly two years after Trump had staged his coup to hold on to the White House—and three days after he had declared his candidacy to retake it.

Which is to say that Garland and the Biden administration, by resisting until the last moment the effort to investigate and punish the instigators of the coup, had contrived to let the story of Trump’s struggle against prosecution and the story of his effort to recapture the White House become one story. Would the former president become the first in history to be indicted? Would he become the first to be convicted? Would he be able to delay his trial until after the election? Would he spend his next years in the White House or in the penitentiary? “That is a vastly different kind of politics,” observes Michael Wolff in All or Nothing: How Trump Recaptured America, “the man on the tightrope without a net.”

Who can take their eyes off him? As Trump’s third presidential campaign came to life…and as the stakes for him became crystal clear, his proposition as a candidate playing both hero and martyr became utterly straightforward: Elect me or destroy me.

Perhaps Trump’s greatest skill as a politician is his ability to tell stories, and the Biden administration had just given him a momentous one: the story of his martyrdom. First the powers that be had stolen the election, and now they were trying to put him in jail. It was a tale of persecution and resentment and grievance—dark emotions that his supporters broadly shared. Had they too not suffered at the hands of the nefarious elites who had shipped their jobs to China? Had not the elites thrown open the border so that illegal immigrants could steal the jobs that were left? Had not the usurper Democratic president brought terrible inflation that had stolen their savings and made their lives unaffordable? And was not Trump showing every day that he knew what it was to be unfairly harmed and hounded by the powers that be? He did know how they felt, he would tell his exultant crowds, and the only way for them to fight back was to vote for him: “They’re after you, I just happen to be standing in the way.” Or, in a piquant variation that Wolff quotes, “Our country is being destroyed, and the only thing standing between you and its obliteration is me.”

Can any election in American history match 2024 in sheer insanity? On a television debate stage in Atlanta, barely 130 days before the vote, the incumbent Democratic president collapsed into geriatric incoherence and in the days after was forced to give way to his far less well known vice-president. The Republican challenger (and former president), meanwhile, was indicted four times on federal and state felony charges, including obstructing an official proceeding and conspiring to defraud the government, and convicted in New York of thirty-four felonies tied to covering up his affair with a porn star. His unrepentant mug shot from Atlanta—he was booked there on a RICO rap for interfering in the election—became a treasured artifact of the campaign. So, too, did a Supreme Court decision, written by Chief Justice John Roberts, granting the president almost unqualified immunity for acts committed within the ambit of his official duties. The decision by the Court to intervene, together with the federal government’s two-year delay in investigating and indicting him, made it impossible to try him for the coup before the election. Would a jury have convicted him? We will never know because the American people in their wisdom went ahead and elected the defendant their forty-seventh president. The federal felony charges were withdrawn.

There are many ways to understand the 2024 election, but one begins with the perception that Trump was a former president who simply had the better story to tell. He dominated the news from what he denounced as his “Stalinist show trials,” holding impromptu press conferences in the courthouse hallways. He lost many of these cases, of course, not only the porn star case but the E. Jean Carroll defamation suits and the business fraud suits in New York, and he often seemed to go out of his way to alienate prosecutors and judges with his antics. Actually, though, Wolff reminds us, “for drama, his courtroom appearances were serving as a better debate replacement.”

He is hardly even playing the game at hand. He, and perhaps only he, is seeing a much larger game: The legal strategy is the media strategy; the media strategy is the legal strategy.

The goal is not to hide or minimize the legal peril, but to bring it on. Combine everything: It’s all part of one big witch hunt. It’s all part of one big election interference. The goal is to hammer DAs, judges, Jack Smith, and primary opponents—it’s the system against him.

Trump recognizes that every indictment juices his fundraising and raises him in the polls and that, as Wolff puts it, “he wins this trial, whatever its outcome,” “if he wins this election.” But it is a tightrope walk, and the over-the-shoulder point of view in this book is from some point on the rope itself. “Can you believe this shit?” Wolff quotes Trump as saying. “They are literally trying to put me in jail. That’s actually pretty cool. I’m like Nelson Mandela. I’m ready, I’ll do fine, and you send me to jail, I’m guaranteed to be president.”

The indictments, the prosecutors, the courts: all of it is a dramatic media machine, allowing him to dominate every news cycle as the heroic martyr, enacted and reenacted. “Trumpian politics is an act of cruelty,” Wolff writes. “He’s a deranged comic with a rapt audience.” The anger, the defiance, the aggression are constant, and for his aggrieved partisans both satisfying and cathartic. Trump proves, however much democracy advocates may resist admitting it, that the more powerful appeal is often to voters’ darker natures. “He rises,” writes Wolff, “in his own mind as well as in the polls, as a function of how much he can trash an opponent.” To discuss Trump in policy terms—as the candidate who won, for example, by promising to tame inflation—takes too literally what people tell pollsters, for Trump as always ran on few real policies, Wolff writes:

Trump is often just a raw nerve, his own rage, resentments, and personal grievances churning in him and, at any given moment, expressed in his public performances—which is exactly what makes them so compelling and, for the campaign, unpredictable,

The suspense of unpredictability is at the heart of much drama and entertainment, and if the reign of Trump proves anything it is that much of politics, no matter how serious, begins with being unable to look away.

What was true of the campaign, of course, is true of his second presidency. More so, really, because that “raw nerve,” as Trump ages, becomes steadily more visible—indeed, more obtrusive. One is struck once again, in Wolff’s close portrait of Trump regaining the presidency, by how unsuited he is to occupy the office. He is an aberrant pile of instincts and impulses, which largely help him command the fascinated or appalled stares of tens of millions. “He’s just a content machine,” as Senator Chris Murphy put it. “He’s creating an episode every day that you have to tune in to.” These episodes shape the public conversation, however rage filled or erratic or inane and however little they have to do with the national interest. Meanwhile his waning popularity did not stop his grift or his corruption or even much constrain his ability to dominate the supine and still largely terrified Republicans. Sinking poll numbers or not, Trump remains, as Wolff writes,

the truly consummate huckster, unafraid that his misrepresentations might be revealed because he had, up his sleeve, endlessly more of them. Without humility, and with a taste—even a need—for constant battle, he never relented, never even came close to an admission, and hence a true, no less final reckoning always rolled into the future.

Nearly two years later, has that reckoning finally come? For many once willing to support Trump, the act had grown old. Unending tumult could no longer mask high prices and endless war. He had run as a populist but he governed as a gilded, royalist authoritarian, and people struggling to get by noticed. Young people, Latinos, and Blacks watched him break his promises of lower prices and no new wars and abandoned him and his antics in disgust.

Now the consummate huckster has two more years in power. Will he let himself fade into the background, puttering around his ballroom and his grand triumphal arch, or will he charge once again onto center stage to “fight, fight, fight”? Will his unquenchable narcissism permit him to share credit and attention and actually get things done? In the end that man on the tightrope—we have seen this before—will do anything to keep the spotlight fixed only on him.
